- **NativeAOT is a first-class case**, because nothing on the dispatch path needs a JIT to close
  a generic.

## Checklist

1. Add the source generator to handler projects and the composition root.
2. Swap assembly scanning for `AddGenerated()`.
3. Change handler signatures to take `ErgosfareContext`.
4. Rewrite behaviours as interceptors in the right stage.
5. Add `[Weight]` where order was implicit.
6. Build, and work through the diagnostics.
7. Continue with [v2.2 to v2.3](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.2-to-v2.3) and
   [v2.11 to v2.12](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.11-to-v2.12).

guides.title: v2.11 to v2.12
guides.description: The breaking changes in v2.12.0-preview — the publish surface, exception interceptor results, the diagnostic prefix, and the two-parameter pre-interceptors.
guides.body:
Five changes need your attention. Four are compiler errors, so the build tells you where to
look; the fifth is a rename that silently stops matching.

Work through them in this order — the diagnostic rename first, because it decides whether you
can see the others.

## 1. `ERGOSG###` becomes `ERGO###`

Numbers are preserved, so the mapping is one rule: **drop the `SG`.**

```diff
- <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGOSG005</NoWarn>
+ <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGO005</NoWarn>
```

```diff
- dotnet_diagnostic.ERGOSG009.severity = warning
+ dotnet_diagnostic.ERGO009.severity = warning
```

```diff
- [SuppressMessage("Usage", "ERGOSG007", Justification = "…")]
+ [SuppressMessage("Usage", "ERGO007", Justification = "…")]
```

{% aside type="caution" %}
This is the one that bites quietly. A suppression naming the old id simply stops matching, and
the diagnostic comes back — as a **build failure** for the error-severity rules. Search your
solution for `ERGOSG` before anything else: `.editorconfig`, `.csproj`, `Directory.Build.props`,
`#pragma` lines and `[SuppressMessage]` attributes.
{% /aside %}

`ERGOEXP001` and `ERGOEXP002` are untouched.

## 2. The two-parameter pre-interceptors are gone

`ICommandPreInterceptor<TCommand, TModifiedCommand>` and its query and event siblings are
removed.

**Migration is a deletion.** Drop the second type argument:

```diff
- public sealed class NormalizeName : ICommandPreInterceptor<CreateProduct, CreateProduct>
+ public sealed class NormalizeName : ICommandPreInterceptor<CreateProduct>
  {
      public ValueTask<CreateProduct> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
          => ValueTask.FromResult(command with { Name = command.Name.Trim() });
  }
```

The interceptor keeps returning exactly what it returned. The one-parameter form returns the
typed message, and `TCommand` is a contract — anything assignable to it satisfies it — so
returning a *derived* message still works:

```diff
- public sealed class Enrich : ICommandPreInterceptor<PlaceOrder, ValidatedPlaceOrder>
+ public sealed class Enrich : ICommandPreInterceptor<PlaceOrder>
  {
-     public ValueTask<ValidatedPlaceOrder> HandleAsync(PlaceOrder command, ErgosfareContext context)
-         => ValueTask.FromResult(new ValidatedPlaceOrder(command));
+     public ValueTask<PlaceOrder> HandleAsync(PlaceOrder command, ErgosfareContext context)
+         => ValueTask.FromResult<PlaceOrder>(new ValidatedPlaceOrder(command));
  }
```

The second parameter existed from a time when the one-parameter contracts still returned
`object`. Once those started returning the typed message it bought nothing.

If you were using the **event** variant, note it was also the odd one out: alone among the
pre-interceptor contracts it did not carry `IEvent`, so discovery never found it and it had to
be registered by hand. The surviving contract is found normally, so you can drop that manual
registration.

## 3. Typed-result exception interceptors return a non-nullable result

`ICommandExceptionInterceptor<TCommand, TResult>`, `IQueryExceptionInterceptor<TQuery, TResult>`
and their `For<TException>` variants now return `ValueTask<TResult>` rather than
`ValueTask<TResult?>`.

```diff
  public sealed class NotFoundToEmpty : IQueryExceptionInterceptor<GetProduct, ProductDto>
  {
-     public ValueTask<ProductDto?> HandleAsync(
+     public ValueTask<ProductDto> HandleAsync(
          GetProduct query, ProductDto? result, Exception exception, ErgosfareContext context)
      {
          if (exception is NotFoundException)
              return ValueTask.FromResult(ProductDto.Empty);

-         return ValueTask.FromResult<ProductDto?>(null);
+         throw exception;
      }
  }
```

**If you were returning `null` to mean "I did not handle this", rethrow instead.** That is what
an unhandled failure looks like, and it lets the exception surface as it should.

Returning `null` used to make the dispatch return `null` into a non-nullable slot — with the
handler's exception gone, no diagnostic and no throw. The parameter stays nullable, and the
asymmetry is the point: the handler may have thrown before producing anything, so there
genuinely may be no result yet. **Nullable in, non-nullable out.**

The erased core contracts keep their nullable return, because they serve the void lane too,
where an empty slot legitimately reaches this stage as `null`.

An assembly compiled against the older contracts now meets a throw naming both types rather
than the silent default.

## 4. `PublishAsync` loses `throwIfNoHandlerFound` and its `string[]` overloads

```diff
- await mediator.PublishAsync(@event, throwIfNoHandlerFound: true, ct);
+ await mediator.PublishAsync(@event, ct);
```

```diff
- await mediator.PublishAsync(@event, new[] { "audit" }, ct);
+ await mediator.PublishAsync(@event, GroupSet.Of("audit"), ct);
```

The full call takes `IEnumerable<string>?`, which subsumes the array overloads — and keeping
both made `PublishAsync(@event, ["a"], token)` ambiguous.

**Grouped publishing is untouched.** Five of the seven `PublishAsync` overloads still take
groups, as `GroupSet` or `IEnumerable<string>?`, for both `IEvent` messages and plain ones. Only
the `string[]` spelling went — and only on `PublishAsync`: the `string[]` overloads on
`SendAsync` and `QueryAsync` are still there.

**A publish that reaches nobody now returns, unconditionally.** The flag asked the caller to
decide at run time about something the compilation can prove, and measured before removal it
was never passed `true` outside the tests that existed to exercise it.

If you were relying on it to catch a missing subscriber, you now get that earlier — see below.

## 5. A publish nothing subscribes to is a build error

```
error ERGO005: This dispatch of 'OrderShipped' can never reach a handler … so the publish is
guaranteed to reach nobody.
```

Event dispatch sites used to be exempt from the dead-dispatch judgment, on the reasoning that
reaching zero subscribers is a legal no-op. That answers a different question: what happens
when no handler matched *on this call* is the container's business, while this asks whether any
subscriber can **ever** match. Declaring the event and forgetting the subscriber is the ordinary
way to get there, and it used to compile in silence.

**Fix:** write the subscriber, or remove the publish.

**Legitimately suppress it** when the subscriber is registered somewhere the compiler cannot
see — a plugin container loading assemblies at run time, a test host registering by hand.
Suppress at the call site with a reason.

Reaching zero subscribers *at run time* is still legal and still returns.

## Worth knowing, but not breaking

These arrived in the same release and need no migration:

**A plain domain type can be an event.** Writing an `IEventHandler<T>` is what makes `T` an
event, so the project declaring your domain events no longer needs an Ergosfare reference. Your
existing `IEvent` messages keep working unchanged.

**Typed result dispatch.** `SendAsync<TMessage, TResult>` and `DispatchAsync<TMessage, TResult>`
are additive, implemented as default interface methods — an existing `ICommandMediator`
implementation keeps compiling and forwards to its untyped call. Worth adopting for NativeAOT,
where it keeps the construction path off `MakeGenericType`.

**More pipelines get compiled plans.** Two handlers in different groups no longer read as a
contested pipeline, and a message with one direct handler is plannable regardless of what its
base types carry. Nothing to do; some dispatches simply get faster.

**A stream no longer drops `null` elements.** If you worked around that by filtering, you can
stop.

## Checklist

1. Search for `ERGOSG` across the solution and rename.
2. Build. Fix what the compiler reports.
3. Drop the second type argument from any two-parameter pre-interceptor.
4. Replace `return null` in typed-result exception interceptors with `throw exception`.
5. Remove `throwIfNoHandlerFound` arguments, and swap `string[]` group arguments for
   `GroupSet.Of` **on `PublishAsync` only** — `SendAsync` and `QueryAsync` keep theirs.
6. Address any `ERGO005` on a publish — write the subscriber, or suppress with a reason.

guides.title: v2.2 to v2.3
guides.description: The release that removed the runtime registry — what replaced it, and what a manual registration has to look like now.
guides.body:
v2.3 removed the runtime registry. Discovery moved into the build, and with it went the APIs
that only made sense while a registry was assembled at start-up.

If you are coming from further back, do [v1 to v2](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v1-to-v2)
first.

## What went

```text
RegisterFromAssembly(…)      → AddGenerated(), written by the source generator
RegisterDescriptors(…)       → no successor; descriptors are compiled, not assembled
the Registry namespace       → no successor; there is no runtime registry to talk to
```

The reasoning is one sentence: **a registry assembled at start-up cannot be reasoned about at
compile time**, and everything the framework does well now — the frozen composition table, the
compiled plans, the reachability diagnostics — depends on the answer existing before the process
does.

## Reference the generator

This is the step people miss. The generator is what writes `AddGenerated()`, so a project
without it has nothing to call:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator" Version="…">
  <PrivateAssets>all</PrivateAssets>
  <IncludeAssets>runtime; build; native; contentfiles; analyzers; buildtransitive</IncludeAssets>
</PackageReference>
```

It belongs in **every project that declares handlers** and in the **composition root**. The
facade package `Stella.Ergosfare` already references it.

## Replace assembly scanning

```csharp
// Before
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.RegisterFromAssembly(typeof(Program).Assembly)));

// Now
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

`AddGenerated()` names every discovered construct through `typeof`. It covers your own
assembly and every referenced one that references Ergosfare, so the scan you used to configure
by hand is now the default.

Scanning references can be turned off per project:

```xml
<ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences>false</ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences>
```

## Manual registration has to name its type

A hand-written `Register` still works, but the type must be known at compile time:

```csharp
// Fine
.Register<AuditEverything>()
.Register(typeof(AuditEverything))

// ERGO018 — an error
.Register(someTypeComputedAtRunTime)
```

A construct whose type is only known at run time gets no compiled pipeline, no frozen
composition and no plan, so the registration cannot mean what it appears to mean. If you were
registering types from a list, replace the list with explicit calls or a discovery key.

## Conditional registration becomes a discovery key

The registry used to be where "register this only in some deployments" was expressed. That is a
`[DiscoveryKey]` now:

```csharp
[DiscoveryKey("reporting")]
public sealed class RebuildReportsHandler : ICommandHandler<RebuildReports> { … }
```

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(module => module
    .AddGenerated()
    .AddGenerated("reporting.*"))
```

Selections are a union, so chaining overlapping patterns is safe. See
[Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys).

## Mark your composition root, if it is a library

The reachability diagnostics run in the project that sees the whole application, and that
defaults to an executable. A test host or a plugin container has to say so:

```xml
<ErgosfareCompositionRoot>true</ErgosfareCompositionRoot>
```

## Expect new diagnostics

This is the part that surprises people, and it is the point of the release. The build now tells
you things the runtime used to discover:

```
error ERGO005: This dispatch of 'ArchiveOrder' can never reach a handler…
error ERGO010: Message 'PlaceOrder' is claimed by 2 main handlers at the same direct level…
warning ERGO007: Handler 'ReindexProduct' … no dispatch site in the compiled closure can
deliver that message.
```

None of these is new *behaviour* — each describes something that already failed, or already
never ran. They are reported earlier now.

Work through them rather than suppressing them wholesale. `ERGO005` and `ERGO010` in particular
describe calls that throw on their first execution. See
[Working with diagnostics](/ergosfare.docs/best-practices/diagnostics).

{% aside type="note" %}
These were named `ERGOSG###` until v2.12. If you are migrating across both releases, do the
prefix rename as well — see
[v2.11 to v2.12](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.11-to-v2.12).
{% /aside %}

## Checklist

1. Add the source generator reference to every project that declares handlers, and to the root.
2. Replace `RegisterFromAssembly` with `AddGenerated()`.
3. Remove `RegisterDescriptors` calls and any `using` of the Registry namespace.
4. Make every `Register` name its type outright.
5. Move conditional registration to `[DiscoveryKey]` plus a pattern selection.
6. Mark a library composition root with `ErgosfareCompositionRoot`.
7. Build, and work through the diagnostics.

guides.title: Ergosfare
guides.description: A source-generated, high-performance mediator for CQRS-style messaging in .NET — commands, queries and events over one pipeline model.
guides.body:
import { Card, CardGrid } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'; import { StarField } from "../../../components/constellation/starfield.tsx"
A Roslyn generator discovers handlers in your compilation *and* in referenced assemblies, pre-computes their descriptors, and emits `AddGenerated()`. A library's handlers register with no registration code in the library. Generated dispatch roots close executor generics at compile time; pipeline plans pre-close generic handler types. No `MakeGenericType`, no registry scan, no `AsyncLocal` on the hot path. Pooled execution contexts and a `ValueTask`-first surface: 100k sequential dispatches allocate 2.3 MB, against MediatR's 18.3 MB for the same loop. `context.CreateScope()` gives a handler an isolated child context with inherited cancellation — the pattern ambient-state mediators cannot offer safely. Every construct referenced statically via `typeof`; dispatch roots anchor every generic instantiation, `record struct` messages included. Commands, Queries and Events are independent packages over a shared core. `IModule` is a real extension point — the shipped modules use it too.

guides.title: Native AOT and trimming
guides.description: Why compile-time dispatch makes NativeAOT viable, what still needs care, and how to check before you publish.
guides.body:
Ergosfare treats a published NativeAOT application as a first-class case. The reason is the same
compile-time work everything else rests on: if the shape of a dispatch is decided while you
compile, there is nothing left for it to construct reflectively.

## What makes it work

**No assembly scan.** Discovery happens at compile time, and `AddGenerated()` names every
construct through `typeof` — which is exactly what the trimming analyzers want to see.

**Generic instantiations are closed in generated code.** A dispatch would otherwise have to
close its executor generic with `MakeGenericType`, which only a JIT can answer. The generated
dispatch roots close them ahead of time, so the type the runtime needs already exists in the
published binary.

**Native result carriers name their own adapter.** Binding a result slot used to close an
adapter generic reflectively; the carrier now answers for itself, which removed the majority of
the adapter layer's reflective bindings along with their `IL2055` and `IL3050` suppressions.

**Nothing depends on a type's name.** No convention scanning, so the linker renaming or removing
things cannot break resolution.

## Publishing

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
  <TrimMode>full</TrimMode>
</PropertyGroup>
```

```bash
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64
```

## What still needs care

### Dispatching through a base type

```csharp
IMessage message = await queue.ReadAsync();
await mediator.DispatchAsync(message, ct);
```

The pipeline that runs belongs to the runtime type, which is correct — but the compiler now
cannot see which message arrives, so it cannot prove a root exists for it. If nothing in the
compilation ever names that message concretely, the dispatch falls back to closing its generic
at run time.

Turn on `ERGO009` to find these:

```ini
dotnet_diagnostic.ERGO009.severity = warning
```

Where the types *are* known, name them:

```csharp
var id = await mediator.SendAsync<PlaceOrder, Guid>(command, ct);
```

That is what the typed overloads are for — not throughput, but keeping the construction path off
reflection.

### Generic messages

A generic message's closed forms are not rooted, because an open definition is not a dispatchable
message. `Wrap<int>` and `Wrap<string>` are separate closed types, and the generator has no list
of which ones your application uses.

If you dispatch generic messages under AOT, root them yourself by dispatching each closed form
somewhere the compiler can see, or avoid generic messages on that path.

### Types hidden from discovery

`[ExcludeFromDiscovery]` keeps a type out of bulk registration. It does **not** stop it being
dispatched — and every hidden message your compilation declares is rooted anyway, precisely so a
hidden message does not become the shape that works in development and fails at publish.

Assembly-level exclusion is different: `[assembly: ExcludeFromDiscovery]` says do not look here
at all, and those types are neither registered nor rooted.

### Registrations naming a runtime type

`Register(someComputedType)` cannot be followed by any of this, which is why it is `ERGO018` —
an error rather than a warning.

### Your own code

The framework's dispatch path is reflection-free; your handlers are your own. JSON
serialization, `Activator.CreateInstance`, dynamic proxies and expression compilation all need
the same care they need in any AOT application.

## Checking before you ship

**Publish in CI, and run the binary.** This is the only check that actually proves anything.
Trimming warnings are useful, but the failure mode being avoided here — a generic that cannot be
closed — shows up when the code path executes.

**Exercise every dispatch shape in a smoke test.** A dispatch that is never executed is a
dispatch whose root you never confirmed.

**Read the trimming warnings.** `IL2026`, `IL2055`, `IL3050` from your own code are real; the
framework should contribute none.

## Trimming without AOT

`PublishTrimmed` alone gets most of the size benefit with fewer constraints, and is a good first
step if AOT is not a requirement:

```xml
<PublishTrimmed>true</PublishTrimmed>
```

The handler trim pairs well with it:

```xml
<ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>true</ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>
```

A handler no dispatch in the closure reaches is then left out of the registration entirely —
reported as `ERGO008` so the exclusion is visible — and the linker can drop it. It only applies
to pure handler types; one that also carries interceptor contracts stays registered for those.

{% aside type="caution" %}
The trim is driven by the same reachability judgment as `ERGO007`, so it is only as good as the
compiler's view. A handler dispatched somewhere invisible — reflectively, or from an assembly
without a manifest — would be trimmed too. Suppress `ERGO007` at those types before turning the
trim on, and the exclusion respects the suppression.
{% /aside %}

## Known gaps

Two shapes still reach the reflective arm, and both are tracked:

- **Generic messages**, whose closed forms are never rooted.
- **A hidden message no registration names at all**, which nothing can enumerate.

Neither is a failure in a JIT run. Both are worth knowing about before an AOT publish.

guides.title: Experimental APIs
guides.description: Surfaces that are still moving, what "experimental" commits to, and how to opt in.
guides.body:
Three parts of the framework are marked experimental. They work, they are tested, and they ship —
what is not settled is their **shape**, and using one means accepting that it may change in a
minor release.

Each surface produces a warning with its own diagnostic ID. Suppression is optional unless your project treats warnings as errors. The markers use `Obsolete` with an experimental message and a custom `ERGOEXP` ID; IDEs may also display obsolete styling.

| Id | Surface |
|---|---|
| `ERGOEXP001` | the declarative result-adapter surface |
| `ERGOEXP002` | the plugin surface |
| `ERGOEXP003` | stream input and pipe converters |

## ERGOEXP001 — result adapters

`[ResultAdapter]`, `[IgnoreResultAdapter]`, and `UseDefaultResultAdapter` with its carrier.

What the value channel *does* is settled: a failing pipeline can hand the caller a failed
carrier instead of throwing, and the exception interceptors still see the failure. How it is
*declared* is what may still move.

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .UseDefaultResultAdapter(typeof(ResultAdapter<>))
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

Opt in for the project:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGOEXP001</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

## ERGOEXP002 — plugins

Everything in `Stella.Ergosfare.Plugins.Abstractions` — `[ErgosfarePlugin]`,
`[PipelineInvokable]`, `[PluginServiceFilter]`, the `Hook` and `Module` enums — together with the
module facade the generator emits from them.

For a **consumer**, the surface is one line, and that is where the suppression goes:

```csharp
#pragma warning disable ERGOEXP002
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddTiming()
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
#pragma warning restore ERGOEXP002
```

For a **plugin author**, the whole package is built on it, so the project-wide form is more
practical:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGOEXP002</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

See [Plugins](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/plugins).

## ERGOEXP003 — stream input

`CommandStream<TChunk, TSelf>` and `QueryStream<TChunk, TSelf>` carry metadata as message
properties and input as a bounded, single-consumer asynchronous sequence. `Pipe` starts
production immediately; capacity limits queued items. The root `ErgosfareStream` implements
`IAsyncDisposable`. The explicit `IBufferWriter<T>` staging buffer grows separately, and
`FlushAsync` applies backpressure when publishing staged items.

Use `IPipeConverter<T>` for stateful conversion from a byte stream, and
`IPipeConverter<S,T>` or delegate overloads for per-item conversion. Byte blocks and
UTF-8 line helpers leave the source open. See the
[streaming multipart upload recipe](/ergosfare.docs/preview/recipes/streaming-upload).

Generated output-stream plans send failures directly to the consumer and final stage;
exception interceptors do not turn a failed stream into a replacement result. Early output
disposal reports `StreamOutputDisposedException` to pending input producers and final
interceptors. Explicit context abort still skips finals. Stream-specific post signatures
and cancellation supplied only through output `WithCancellation` remain design work;
pass the cancellation token to mediator dispatch and dispose unused inputs explicitly.

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGOEXP003</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

## What the marker commits to

**It will keep working in the release it shipped in.** Experimental is not unfinished — these
surfaces carry tests like everything else.

**It may change shape in a minor release.** An attribute may be renamed, a parameter added, an
enum member removed. The plugin surface has already been through this once: it had six
addressable stages, two of which let a plugin change a consumer's pipeline structure, and it
was cut back to four observation-only hooks.

**A change will be in the changelog with a migration note.** The two-parameter pre-interceptor
removal is the template — what went, why, and what replaces it.

## Where the line is

Something is experimental when *how you express it* is still being worked out. Once the
spelling has survived real use, the marker comes off and the surface joins the ordinary
compatibility promise.

The rest of the framework — the message contracts, the mediators, interceptors, discovery,
groups, weights — is not experimental and does not change shape in a minor release.

## Should you use them

**Result adapters:** yes, if your application already carries failures as values. It replaces
the try/catch you would write in every handler, and the declaration is the only part that might
move.

**Plugins:** yes for internal packages, where you control both sides and can update together.
For a package published to third parties, weigh it — your consumers inherit the suppression and
the churn.

Either way, pin the exact version. In a preview line a floating reference turns a shape change
into a surprise at restore time.

guides.title: Performance
guides.description: What a dispatch actually does at run time, which pipelines get a compiled plan, and what stops one from being built.
guides.body:
The performance story is a single idea: **do the shape work once, at compile time, and let a
dispatch be the work you asked for.** This page is about what that means concretely, and what
takes a pipeline off the fast path.

## What a dispatch does

For a message with a compiled plan:

1. Look the plan up — one dictionary hit, keyed by message type and group set.
2. Check the plan against the composition the container actually built.
3. Run the plan: a straight line of calls with the interceptors already in place.

There is no reflection, no `MakeGenericType`, no descriptor list to sort, no `AsyncLocal`, and
no context allocation — contexts are pooled and returned when the dispatch completes.

Handler and interceptor *instances* still come from the dispatching scope, because that is what
makes scoped dependencies work. For participants the generator can prove are plain transients
with a single public constructor, even that goes: the plan constructs them with `new`.

## What gets a plan

Three families, in order of how specific they are:

**Single-handler plans** — a message whose whole pipeline is one handler and no interceptors.
The cheapest possible shape.

**Staged plans** — a message with interceptors, emitted as a class whose body is the pipeline
written out. One per `(message, group set)`.

**Broadcast plans** — the same, for a publish that delivers to several subscribers.

Everything else takes the general path, which is correct and measurably slower.

## What stops a plan from being built

A plan is only built when the generator can settle every part of the pipeline. Any of these
leaves a message on the general path:

- A **keyed** participant, whose presence depends on which container was built.
- A **nested** participant type — the runtime orders segments by `Type.FullName`, whose nested
  separator sorts differently from the display name's dot.
- Several registrations reaching the same participant, whose order among its own appearances is
  not modelled.
- An **exception filter** that cannot be reproduced as an `is` test.
- A message declaring **several result contracts**, so the result is named at the call rather
  than by the message.
- `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` on the message.
- A **stream query** — the streaming lane has no plan family.

None of these is a defect. They are cases where the compiler declines to guess, and the general
path handles them correctly.

## The plan is always checked

Before running a plan, the executor compares the composition it was baked against with what the
container composed, segment by segment. A mismatch falls back.

This is what makes the whole mechanism safe rather than clever: a stale or wrong plan costs you
the speedup and never the behaviour.

## Groups and plans

A group set is part of what keys a plan, so a message dispatched under two constant sets gets
two plans — each a straight line with exactly the participants that set selects. Filtering does
not happen per dispatch.

A dispatch naming a set the compiler cannot read gets one plan carrying every participant, with
each one's membership evaluated at run time. Still a compiled plan; it just does the selection
you deferred.

```csharp
await mediator.SendAsync(command, GroupSet.Of("audit"));  // its own plan
await mediator.SendAsync(command, _configured);           // one filtering plan
```

A `static readonly GroupSet` is readable, so naming a set once and reusing it keeps the faster
shape.

## The typed dispatch overloads

Naming both types at a call site:

```csharp
var id = await mediator.SendAsync<PlaceOrder, Guid>(command, ct);
```

This is **not** a throughput optimisation — paired benchmark runs put the typed and untyped
lanes within a nanosecond of each other, in both directions. The untyped lane already answers
in a single dictionary lookup.

What it buys is the **construction path**: the executor closes from arguments the compiler
already resolved, so the arm that would otherwise reach `MakeGenericType` for a message with no
generated root is never taken. That is a NativeAOT concern, not a hot-path one.

## Memoized handlers

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry.ForceMemoizedHandlers());
```

Keeps resolved participants rather than resolving per dispatch. Worth it only when handlers are
genuinely stateless and their dependencies are singletons — a background worker draining a
queue. It is wrong anywhere a handler depends on something scoped, because the captured instance
outlives the scope that produced it.

## Where the remaining cost is

**Your handler.** Once the pipeline is a straight line, what is left is the work you wrote.

**Container resolution**, for participants that could not be proven directly constructible.
`ERGO003` tells you when several public constructors are the reason.

**Broad interceptors.** One written against `ICommand` runs for every command *and* every nested
dispatch. That is a design cost; narrowing the contract is the fix.

## Measuring it

The repository carries a BenchmarkDotNet suite covering each lane, including paired typed and
untyped runs so the claims above stay checkable rather than remembered.

For your own application, measure the dispatch against a direct method call on the same handler.
The gap is the framework's cost, and it should be small enough to be uninteresting next to
whatever the handler does.

{% aside type="tip" %}
Before optimising anything here, check whether your messages get plans at all. Dump the
generated file and look — a `StagedPlan` class for your message means the fast path is in play,
and its absence usually points at one of the reasons listed above.
{% /aside %}

guides.title: Plugins
guides.description: Shipping cross-cutting behaviour as a package — the four hooks, plugin options, and what a plugin deliberately cannot do.
guides.body:
A plugin is a NuGet package that observes pipelines. Install it, and its code runs at named
points inside every dispatch the consuming application makes — with no registration to write
and no interceptor to wire up.

{% aside type="caution" %}
The plugin surface is experimental and marked `ERGOEXP002`. Installing a plugin is the one line
of it you write yourself, and it is where the suppression goes. See
[Experimental APIs](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/experimental-apis).
{% /aside %}

## Installing one

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddTiming()
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

`AddTiming()` is generated into the plugin's own assembly, so the consumer calls an ordinary
extension method. If the plugin declares options, the call takes them:

```csharp
.AddTiming(new TimingOptions { Threshold = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200) })
```

That is the whole consumer surface.

## Writing one

Two things make an assembly a plugin: an assembly attribute naming it, and at least one method
marked with a hook.

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Plugins.Abstractions;

[assembly: ErgosfarePlugin("Timing")]
```

The name becomes the generated `TimingModule` and the `AddTiming()` extension, so pick
something that reads well at a call site.

```csharp
public sealed class TimingService(ILogger<TimingService> logger)
{
    [PipelineInvokable(Hook.PreMain)]
    public void BeforeHandler<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context)
        => context.Set("startedAt", Stopwatch.GetTimestamp());

    [PipelineInvokable(Hook.PostMain)]
    public void AfterHandler<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        if (context.TryGet<long>("startedAt", out var started))
            logger.LogInformation("{Message} took {Elapsed}",
                typeof(TMessage).Name, Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(started));
    }
}
```

The class is registered as a singleton by the generated module. Its constructor dependencies
are resolved from the container, so a plugin service takes ordinary dependencies.

## The four hooks

```
Start → pre* → PreMain → handler → PostMain → post* → Finish
```

| Hook | Where it runs |
|---|---|
| `Hook.Start` | at the very beginning of the dispatch |
| `Hook.PreMain` | after the pre-interceptors, before the handler |
| `Hook.PostMain` | after the handler, before the post-interceptors |
| `Hook.Finish` | at the end of a successful dispatch |

Every one of them is a **straight-line position that exists in every pipeline**. That is the
design constraint the whole surface is built around: no plan grows a `try`, a `catch` or a
`finally` because a plugin was installed. An interceptorless pipeline carrying calls at all four
hooks is still the straight line it is without them.

Points coincide rather than disappear. With no pre-interceptors, `Start` and `PreMain` name the
same instant and both calls run. In a broadcast, `PreMain` and `PostMain` name the seam around
a *delivery*, so they run once per subscriber.

## What a plugin cannot do

**It cannot see the failure path.** There is no hook on the exception or final stages, and this
is deliberate: those stages are what force a pipeline to carry a `try`/`finally`, and a
third-party package should not be able to change the shape of a consumer's pipeline by being
installed.

A plugin that genuinely needs the failure path ships an interceptor instead — a plugin package
can contain one like any other assembly, and the consumer's composition already knows how to
place it.

**It cannot change the message or the result.** A hook method returns `void` or `ValueTask`.
Hooks observe; interceptors participate.

## One signature, whatever the pipeline produces

A hook method takes one type parameter — its message — and nothing else varies:

```csharp
[PipelineInvokable(Hook.Start)]
public ValueTask OnStart<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context) { … }
```

No hook carries a result, so a void command, a result-producing query and an event broadcast
all call the same method the same way. A `void` method is called plainly and never enters the
state machine; a `ValueTask` one is awaited.

Parameters are filled positionally: the message from the dispatch, the `ErgosfareContext` from
the pipeline, and anything else resolved from the container.

## Narrowing where a hook runs

A generic constraint is how a plugin says which messages it applies to:

```csharp
[PipelineInvokable(Hook.PreMain)]
public void OnOrder<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context)
    where TMessage : IOrderMessage { … }
```

The call is closed over each plan's concrete types when it is written, so a constraint is both a
selection rule and something the emitted code has to satisfy. A constraint that cannot be
reproduced from type names — a constructed generic, `new()`, `unmanaged` — makes the whole
method unmodelable and it is passed over rather than guessed at.

`[PluginServiceFilter]` narrows by module family or discovery key:

```csharp
[PluginServiceFilter(Module.Command | Module.Query)]
public sealed class TimingService { … }
```

A method-level filter narrows the type's rather than replacing it: families intersect, and keys
add together.

## Plugin options

Name an options type in the assembly attribute:

```csharp
[assembly: ErgosfarePlugin("Timing", typeof(TimingOptions))]

public sealed class TimingOptions
{
    public TimeSpan Threshold { get; init; } = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100);
}
```

`AddTiming()` now takes an instance, and the module hands it to the service it constructs.

**The options never enter the container.** Nothing registers them, no resolution looks them up,
and the consumer constructs what they pass — so there is no builder in between and nothing
configurable the call site cannot see.

There are two ways for a service to receive them, chosen by what you write.

**Write a constructor.** It is left alone, and its other parameters are still resolved from the
container:

```csharp
public sealed class TimingService(TimingOptions options, ILogger<TimingService> logger) { … }
```

**Or make the class `partial` and write none.** The generator writes the field and the line that
assigns it:

```csharp
public sealed partial class TimingService
{
    [PipelineInvokable(Hook.Finish)]
    public void OnFinish<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context)
        => _logger.LogInformation("threshold {T}", _options.Threshold);
}
```

A service that is neither — no constructor and not `partial`, or several public constructors —
is `ERGO017`, rather than silently ignoring settings its own plugin declared.

## Packaging

A plugin is an ordinary library that references `Stella.Ergosfare.Plugins.Abstractions` and the
source generator. The generator emits the module and the registry extension into the plugin's
own compilation, so nothing about this depends on one generator seeing another's output.

{% aside type="danger" %}
**Do not name a plugin assembly `Stella.Ergosfare.*`.** That prefix is reserved, and reference
scanning skips it — Ergosfare's own contract interfaces inherit the module markers and would
otherwise all register as user types. A plugin under the prefix would silently reach no
pipeline at all, so it is reported as `ERGO015`.

If you genuinely must live under the prefix, opt back in per assembly:

```csharp
[assembly: AssemblyMetadata("ErgosfareSourceGeneratorForceScanReferences", "true")]
```
{% /aside %}

## What it costs

Nothing while nothing is installed, and nothing structural when something is. A hook call is a
call at a point the pipeline already had. The plugin service is a singleton resolved once per
container, not per dispatch, and its per-dispatch dependencies arrive as method parameters —
which is why the lifetime is fixed rather than left to the author.

guides.title: Composition root and testing
guides.description: Where registration belongs, how to lay projects out so discovery works for you, and how to test a pipeline without mocking the mediator.
guides.body:
## One composition root

Register once, in the project that becomes your application. That is where the generator judges
reachability, because it is the only place that sees the whole closure — which is why `ERGO005`
and `ERGO007` appear when you build the executable rather than the library that declared the
handler.

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

If your root is a library rather than an executable — a test host, a plugin container, a
function app — say so, or the judgments never run:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ErgosfareCompositionRoot>true</ErgosfareCompositionRoot>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Splitting registration across several places is the main way people lose the diagnostics.
Everything the compiler can tell you depends on one project seeing the whole picture.

## Laying projects out

A layout that works with discovery rather than against it:

```
MyApp.Domain            ← domain types, plain events. No Ergosfare reference.
MyApp.Application       ← messages, handlers, interceptors. Abstractions + generator.
MyApp.Infrastructure    ← implementations the handlers depend on.
MyApp.Api               ← composition root. Extensions + generator.
```

Three things make this work:

**Messages live with their handlers**, in the application layer. A message and the code that
serves it change together.

**Domain events stay plain.** A subscriber is what makes a type an event, so `MyApp.Domain` can
declare `OrderShipped` with no reference to anything.

**The generator is referenced in both the application layer and the root.** In the library it
finds handlers and records what that assembly dispatches; in the root it writes the registration
and runs the judgments.

## Libraries that ship handlers

A library's handlers register through the application that consumes it — the reference scan
finds them, and the library ships no registration code.

Two things to get right:

**Grant access to internal handlers**, or they are invisible to the consumer's generated code:

```csharp
[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("MyApp.Api")]
```

Otherwise they surface as `ERGO002`. Making them `public` is the other answer.

**Give optional handlers a discovery key**, so a consumer opts in rather than getting them
whether they wanted them or not:

```csharp
[DiscoveryKey("myLibrary.optional")]
public sealed class OptionalHandler : ICommandHandler<Something> { … }
```

## Testing: build the real pipeline

The instinct to mock `ICommandMediator` is worth resisting. A mocked mediator tests that your
code called a mediator — it does not test that a handler exists, that its interceptors run, or
that the dispatch resolves at all. Those are exactly the things that break.

Build a container instead. It is a few lines, and it is the real thing:

```csharp
private static IServiceProvider BuildHost()
{
    var services = new ServiceCollection();

    services.AddSingleton<IOrderRepository, InMemoryOrderRepository>();
    services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
        .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
        .AddEventModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));

    return services.BuildServiceProvider();
}

[Fact]
public async Task PlacingAnOrder_ReturnsItsId()
{
    using var scope = BuildHost().CreateScope();
    var mediator = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ICommandMediator>();

    var id = await mediator.SendAsync(new PlaceOrder(customerId, lines));

    Assert.NotEqual(Guid.Empty, id);
}
```

This runs the pipeline your application runs: the same handler selection, the same interceptors,
the same order.

{% aside type="tip" %}
Mark the test project a composition root. Then the reachability diagnostics run over your test
assembly too, and a test dispatching a message with no handler fails at build rather than at
run time.
{% /aside %}

## Testing a handler on its own

A handler is an ordinary class, so when you want to test its logic and nothing else, construct
it:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task Handler_SavesTheOrder()
{
    var repository = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    var handler = new PlaceOrderHandler(repository, new FlatPricing());

    var id = await handler.HandleAsync(new PlaceOrder(customerId, lines),
                                       new ErgosfareContext());

    Assert.Single(repository.Saved);
}
```

Use both kinds. The unit test pins the logic; the container test pins that the logic is
reachable.

## Testing an interceptor

Through the pipeline, because ordering and matching are the parts worth testing. Register a
handler that records what it saw, dispatch, and assert on the effect:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task PreInterceptor_TrimsTheName()
{
    using var scope = BuildHost().CreateScope();
    var mediator = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ICommandMediator>();
    var spy = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<RecordingRepository>();

    await mediator.SendAsync(new CreateProduct("  Bench  ", 10m));

    Assert.Equal("Bench", spy.Last.Name);
}
```

Testing an interceptor by calling `HandleAsync` directly tells you the body works. It does not
tell you the interceptor is reached, which is usually the failure you are guarding against.

## Isolating tests from each other

Handler instances come from the dispatching scope, so a scope per test gives each one its own
scoped services:

```csharp
using var scope = provider.CreateScope();
```

Avoid `ForceMemoizedHandlers()` in tests unless you are specifically testing it. It keeps
resolved participants, which is exactly the state leak you do not want between cases.

## Before you ship

**Build the composition root with warnings as errors.** That is where the reachability
judgments run, and where `ERGO007` catches the handler whose dispatch you removed last week.

**If you publish NativeAOT, publish it in CI.** The compile-time work is what makes AOT viable,
but the way to know is to publish and run — see
[Native AOT and trimming](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/aot-and-trimming).

guides.title: Working with diagnostics
guides.description: Every ERGO code, what it is telling you, and when suppressing one is the right answer.
guides.body:
Ergosfare's diagnostics are not style advice. Most of them report something that will go wrong
at run time, proved at compile time — so the default posture is to fix them, and suppressing
one should be a decision you can explain.

They come in two families: `ERGO###` for what the generator can prove about your code, and
`ERGOEXP###` marking a surface that is still moving.

## The errors

These fail the build, because each one describes a call that cannot work.

### ERGO005 — this dispatch can never reach a handler

Neither the dispatched type nor any subtype in the compiled closure has a handler.

```csharp
await mediator.SendAsync(new ArchiveOrder(id));   // nothing handles ArchiveOrder
```

**Fix:** write the handler, or delete the dispatch. It applies to publishing too — an event no
subscriber serves is a dead dispatch, and writing the event while forgetting the subscriber is
the ordinary way to get there.

**Legitimately suppress it** when the handler is registered somewhere the compiler cannot see:
a plugin container loading assemblies at run time, a test host registering by hand. Suppress at
the call site with a reason.

### ERGO010 — two handlers claim one message

A command or query has exactly one handler, and the priority ladder has no tiebreaker within a
level.

**Fix:** delete one; make one direct so it wins outright; or separate them by group or
discovery key if they are genuinely alternatives.

### ERGO011 / ERGO012 — result adapter annotations

`ERGO011` is a `[ResultAdapter]` naming an adapter that can never bind — it does not implement
the contract for any slot the message dispatches, or cannot be instantiated. `ERGO012` is a
message carrying both `[ResultAdapter]` and `[IgnoreResultAdapter]`, which asks for two
opposite things.

### ERGO013 — a result no adapter serves

You configured a default result adapter, which makes value-carried failure the application's
contract — and this message's result cannot take part, so its pipeline keeps throwing.

**Fix:** return a carrier the adapter serves, declare a `[ResultAdapter]` for the message, or
acknowledge it with `[IgnoreResultAdapter]`, which turns it into the `ERGO014` warning instead.

### ERGO018 — a registration naming a runtime type

```csharp
registry.Register(typeof(T).Assembly.GetTypes().First());   // ERGO018
```

The closed world compiles a construct's pipeline, freezes its composition and bakes its plan
from what the compilation can see. A type known only at run time enters none of that, so the
registration cannot mean what it appears to.

**Fix:** `Register<T>()` or `Register(typeof(T))` with a concrete type, or let
`AddGenerated()` collect it.

## The warnings

### ERGO001 / ERGO002 — a type that cannot be named

`ERGO001` is a `private`, `protected` or file-local type in your own code. `ERGO002` is an
`internal` type in a referenced assembly with no `InternalsVisibleTo` grant for you.

**Fix:** make it `internal` at least, or grant access. Both say the declaration promises
something its accessibility takes back.

### ERGO006 — only subtypes are handled

The dispatched static type is a concrete message with no handler, while a subtype has one. An
instance of exactly that type throws.

**Fix:** usually the base type should be `abstract`. If instances of it are real, it needs its
own handler.

### ERGO007 — a handler nothing can reach

No dispatch in the compiled closure can deliver this handler's message.

**Fix:** it is usually dead code — the dispatch was renamed or removed. If the registration is
deliberate, suppress it at the type with a reason, or turn on the trim:

```xml
<ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>true</ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>
```

which reports `ERGO008` for each handler it excludes instead.

### ERGO015 — a plugin under the reserved prefix

A plugin assembly named `Stella.Ergosfare.*` is skipped by reference scanning, so none of its
hooks reach any pipeline.

**Fix:** rename it. If you must keep the name, opt back in with
`[assembly: AssemblyMetadata("ErgosfareSourceGeneratorForceScanReferences", "true")]`.

### ERGO016 — a generic participant that closes over nothing

Its contract names a bare type parameter as the message, so no concrete message can bind it:

```csharp
public sealed class ValidateAnything<TCommand> : ICommandPreInterceptor<TCommand>
    where TCommand : ICommand { … }
```

It registers and never runs, which is the worst shape a validation or authorization interceptor
can take.

**Fix:** declare it over the message type or a base contract such as `ICommand`. If the
constraint admits compiled messages, they are closed over automatically and this never fires.

### ERGO017 — a plugin service that cannot receive its options

No constructor to pass them to, several public constructors, or not `partial`.

**Fix:** write a constructor taking the options type, or mark the class `partial` and let the
generator write the field for you.

## The informational ones

These cost you nothing at run time. They report a fast path you did not get.

**ERGO003** — a handler with several public constructors. Which one the container picks depends
on what is registered, so direct construction cannot be proven equivalent. Collapse to one
public constructor to get it.

**ERGO004** — `[FromServices]` on a constructor parameter, where it does nothing. Constructor
injection resolves services with or without it. Remove it; for keyed services use
`[FromKeyedServices]`.

**ERGO008** — a handler the trim excluded. Visible so the exclusion is on record.

**ERGO009** — an opaque dispatch site, off by default. The static type at the call — `object`,
`IMessage`, a bare marker — proves nothing about which message arrives, so reachability can only
reason in aggregate there. Turn it on when you want every dispatch provable:

```ini
dotnet_diagnostic.ERGO009.severity = warning
```

## How to suppress one properly

Narrowly, and with a reason. Prefer the attribute at the exact site over a project-wide
`NoWarn`:

```csharp
[SuppressMessage("Usage", "ERGO007",
    Justification = "Dispatched by the integration test host, which registers by hand.")]
public sealed class ReplayHandler : ICommandHandler<Replay> { … }
```

A project-wide suppression is worth it only for a whole category you have decided against —
and it belongs in the project file with a comment saying why.

{% aside type="caution" %}
`ERGO005` and `ERGO010` are errors on purpose. Suppressing one without understanding it means
shipping a call that throws on its first execution. If you are reaching for `NoWarn` on either,
check first that the handler really is registered somewhere the compiler cannot see.
{% /aside %}

## The experimental markers

`ERGOEXP001` marks the result-adapter surface and `ERGOEXP002` the plugin surface. They are not
findings — they say the API is still moving and using it is opting into that.

Suppress them where you opt in, which for a plugin is the one `Add<Name>()` line:

```csharp
#pragma warning disable ERGOEXP002
registry.AddTiming();
#pragma warning restore ERGOEXP002
```

See [Experimental APIs](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/experimental-apis).

## Keeping a build honest

Two habits are worth having:

**Treat warnings as errors in CI**, so `ERGO006`, `ERGO007` and `ERGO016` cannot accumulate.

**Turn on `ERGO009` before an AOT push.** Opaque dispatch sites are exactly where the compiler
stops being able to prove things, and where a NativeAOT publish is most likely to differ from
your development run.

guides.title: Interceptor or handler
guides.description: Where cross-cutting work belongs, which stage to put it in, and the cases where an interceptor is the wrong tool.
guides.body:
An interceptor is for work that is **about** a dispatch rather than **part of** it. Logging,
authorization, validation, metrics, retries — things you would otherwise write again in every
handler.

The test that settles most cases: *would you have to copy this into the next handler you write?*
If yes, it is cross-cutting. If it only makes sense for this one message, it belongs in the
handler.

## Which stage

| You want to | Stage |
|---|---|
| reject, enrich or rewrite before the work | **pre** |
| shape or wrap a successful result | **post** |
| translate a failure into a result | **exception** |
| always observe the outcome | **final** |

### Pre

Anything that decides whether the work should happen at all, or fixes up the message first:

```csharp
public sealed class RequireTenant : ICommandPreInterceptor
{
    public ValueTask<object> HandleAsync(ICommand command, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        if (_tenant.Current is null)
            context.Abort("no tenant on this request");

        return ValueTask.FromResult<object>(command);
    }
}
```

Use `context.Abort()` rather than throwing your own exception when the answer is "this dispatch
should not continue". An abort skips the exception *and* final stages and travels to the caller
unchanged; a thrown exception runs the failure path, which is a different thing to say.

### Post

Result shaping that is not the handler's business — enveloping, cache population, an outbox
append:

```csharp
public sealed class CacheProduct : IQueryPostInterceptor<GetProduct, ProductDto>
{
    public ValueTask<ProductDto> HandleAsync(
        GetProduct query, ProductDto result, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        _cache.Set(query.Id, result);
        return ValueTask.FromResult(result);
    }
}
```

### Exception

Translating a failure into an answer the caller can use:

```csharp
public sealed class NotFoundToEmpty
    : IQueryExceptionInterceptorFor<GetProduct, ProductDto, NotFoundException>
{
    public ValueTask<ProductDto> HandleAsync(
        GetProduct query, ProductDto? result, NotFoundException exception, ErgosfareContext context)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(ProductDto.Empty);
}
```

Only claim a failure you can actually answer. The result goes out non-nullable because the
caller locked its result type at the call site — an interceptor that has nothing to return
should rethrow and let the exception surface, not invent an empty value to satisfy the
signature.

### Final

Anything that must happen either way — timing, releasing something, an audit row:

```csharp
public sealed class RecordOutcome : ICommandFinalInterceptor
{
    public ValueTask HandleAsync(
        IMessage message, object? result, Exception? exception, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        _metrics.Record(message.GetType().Name, succeeded: exception is null);
        return ValueTask.CompletedTask;
    }
}
```

Remember it does not run after an abort. If you need cleanup on *every* exit including a
deliberate stop, do it in the handler with `try`/`finally` where you can see it.

## Scope it as narrowly as it is true

Three arities, and the widest one is rarely the right answer:

```csharp
ICommandPreInterceptor                  // every command
ICommandPreInterceptor<OrderCommand>    // one hierarchy
ICommandPreInterceptor<PlaceOrder>      // one message
```

A validation interceptor written against `ICommand` runs for every command in the application,
including the ones that need no validation, and including nested dispatches. Narrowing it to a
base type you own keeps the cost where the value is — and gives you the typed message, which is
worth having anyway.

## Ordering is `[Weight]`, and it is worth being explicit

Within a stage, order is weight descending, then direct before covariant. When two interceptors
genuinely depend on order — authorize before validate, correlate before log — say so:

```csharp
[Weight(100)] public sealed class Authorize : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
[Weight(50)]  public sealed class Validate  : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
```

Leaving both at the default and relying on the tiebreaker means a rename can reorder your
pipeline.

## Groups, for pipelines that differ per call

When a subset of interceptors should run only sometimes, that is a group rather than a flag:

```csharp
[Group("audit")]
public sealed class WriteAuditRow : ICommandFinalInterceptor { … }
```

```csharp
await mediator.SendAsync(command, GroupSet.Of("audit"));
```

An interceptor with no group belongs to the default group and runs on an ungrouped dispatch.
See [Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/preview/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

## When an interceptor is the wrong tool

**When it needs to know the specific message to do its job.** An interceptor written against
`ICommand` that switches on the concrete type is a handler with extra steps, and it will keep
growing.

**When the behaviour is really a decorator on a dependency.** Retry, circuit-breaking and
caching for one service belong on that service, where they apply whoever calls it — not on
every dispatch that happens to reach it.

**When the work belongs to a request, not a dispatch.** Interceptors run per dispatch, and one
request can make several. Something that must happen once per request belongs in middleware.

**When you need the failure path from a plugin.** A plugin's hooks deliberately do not cover
the exception and final stages, because they are what force a pipeline to carry a
`try`/`finally`. Ship an interceptor in the plugin package instead — see
[Plugins](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/plugins).

## What interceptors cost

For a pipeline whose shape is settled, the compiled plan is a straight line with the calls in
place — no descriptor list, no ordering at run time. The cost is the work you wrote, not the
mechanism around it.

The one thing worth watching is a broad interceptor doing expensive work: written against
`ICommand`, it runs for every command *and* every nested dispatch. That is a design cost rather
than a framework one, and narrowing the contract is the fix.

guides.title: Messages and handlers
guides.description: Shaping messages so the compiler can help you — command or query, IEvent or a plain type, what a result should carry, and where a handler stops.
guides.body:
Most of what makes an Ergosfare application pleasant to work in is decided when you write the
message, not when you write the handler. These are the calls worth making deliberately.

## Command or query

The line is whether the caller is asking for something to happen or asking what is true.

**A command is an instruction.** It changes state, it has exactly one handler, and its result —
if it has one — is the *outcome of doing it*: the id that was created, the receipt.

**A query changes nothing.** It has exactly one handler and its result is the answer.

```csharp
public sealed record PlaceOrder(Guid CustomerId, IReadOnlyList<Line> Lines) : ICommand<Guid>;
public sealed record GetOrder(Guid Id) : IQuery<OrderDto>;
```

When a command's result starts looking like a projection — the whole entity, a page of rows —
that is usually two operations wearing one name. Return the id and let the caller query.

## `IEvent` or a plain type

An event message does not have to implement anything. Writing an `IEventHandler<OrderShipped>`
is what makes `OrderShipped` an event, so you have a real choice:

```csharp
// a plain domain type — no Ergosfare reference where it is declared
public sealed record OrderShipped(Guid Id, DateTimeOffset At);

// or one that declares itself
public sealed record OrderShipped(Guid Id, DateTimeOffset At) : IEvent;
```

**Use a plain type when the event belongs to your domain.** A domain event is a fact about your
business, and the project that declares it should not need a mediator reference to say so. This
is the better default for anything in a domain or contracts assembly.

**Use `IEvent` when the type exists to be dispatched.** An integration event, a message shaped
for a queue, something with no meaning outside the pipeline — declaring the marker documents
that, and it makes the type discoverable on its own rather than only through a subscriber.

The mechanics are identical either way. What differs is which assembly ends up referencing
Ergosfare, and that is an architecture question rather than a framework one.

{% aside type="note" %}
A plain type is classified through the subscriber that names it, so it works across assembly
boundaries too — the subscriber can live anywhere. What it cannot do is be *found* without one:
a plain type nobody subscribes to is simply a class.
{% /aside %}

## Make messages records, and keep them immutable

```csharp
public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name, decimal Price) : ICommand<Guid>;
```

A pre-interceptor may rewrite the message, and `with` makes that a one-liner that cannot
accidentally mutate what an earlier stage already saw:

```csharp
=> ValueTask.FromResult(command with { Name = command.Name.Trim() });
```

`sealed` is worth the keystrokes: an unsealed message invites a subtype, and a subtype changes
which handler serves it.

## Avoid `struct` messages

A value type has no contract variance, so a struct message reaches only registrations that name
it exactly. Every cross-cutting interceptor you have written against `ICommand` silently skips
it, and no warning is coming — that is how the runtime works, and the compile-time judgments
apply the same rule.

The allocation you save is one small object per dispatch. It is almost never worth the
surprise.

## Name the result type the caller actually needs

A result is a contract. Returning your entity ties every caller to your persistence model:

```csharp
// leaks the aggregate
public sealed record GetOrder(Guid Id) : IQuery<Order>;

// a shape you own on purpose
public sealed record GetOrder(Guid Id) : IQuery<OrderDto>;
```

For a command, prefer the narrowest thing that is genuinely useful. `ICommand<Guid>` is a
better contract than `ICommand<Order>` when the caller only ever needed the id.

## One result type per message

A message declaring several result contracts cannot be given a compiled plan, because the
result is then named at the call site rather than by the message. It still works — it just
takes the general path.

```csharp
// works, but no plan
public sealed record Ambiguous : ICommand<Guid>, ICommand<string>;
```

If you find yourself here, you have two messages.

## Where a handler stops

A handler orchestrates. It should read as a short description of the operation, and delegate
the parts that are not orchestration:

```csharp
public sealed class PlaceOrderHandler(IOrderRepository repository, IPricing pricing)
    : ICommandHandler<PlaceOrder, Guid>
{
    public async ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(PlaceOrder command, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        var order = Order.Create(command.CustomerId, command.Lines, pricing);
        await repository.AddAsync(order, context.CancellationToken);
        return order.Id;
    }
}
```

Three things do not belong in it:

**Cross-cutting work** — logging, validation, authorization, metrics. That is what interceptors
are for, and putting it in the handler means writing it again in the next handler. See
[Interceptor or handler](/ergosfare.docs/preview/best-practices/interceptor-or-handler).

**Business rules that belong to the domain.** If the handler is deciding *what is allowed*
rather than *what to call*, the rule probably wants to live on the aggregate.

**Another dispatch you could have made a method call.** Nested dispatch is legitimate, but a
handler that dispatches three messages you own, in the same layer, has bought indirection
without decoupling.

## Pass the cancellation token down

```csharp
await repository.AddAsync(order, context.CancellationToken);
```

Every async call in a handler should take it. This is the single most common omission, and it
only shows up under load.

## One handler per message, and let the compiler enforce it

Two handlers claiming one message at the same level is `ERGO010` — a build error, because the
priority ladder has no tiebreaker within a level and every dispatch would throw.

The legitimate shapes are:

**A default with an override.** A handler on the base type, a handler on the derived one. The
direct registration wins outright, with no ambiguity.

```csharp
public sealed class OrderCommandHandler : ICommandHandler<OrderCommand> { … }  // fallback
public sealed class PlaceOrderHandler   : ICommandHandler<PlaceOrder>   { … }  // wins
```

**Different groups**, when the two are alternatives selected per dispatch.

**Different discovery keys**, when they belong to different deployments.

What is not legitimate is two handlers you intended to be one. That is what the error is for.

## Let unreachable code be reported

`ERGO007` says a handler no dispatch can reach. It is worth treating as a real finding rather
than noise: usually it means the dispatch was renamed, the feature was removed, or the message
is dispatched somewhere the compiler cannot see.

If the registration is deliberate — a handler dispatched reflectively by a test host, say —
suppress it at the type with a reason, so the next reader knows it was a decision.

guides.title: Defining a command
guides.description: Declaring a command with or without a result, and what the choice commits you to.
guides.body:
A command is an instruction: it changes state, exactly one handler serves it, and it either
produces a result or it does not.

## With no result

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions;

public sealed record ArchiveOrder(Guid Id) : ICommand;
```

## With a result

```csharp
public sealed record PlaceOrder(Guid CustomerId, IReadOnlyList<Line> Lines) : ICommand<Guid>;
```

`ICommand<TResult>` extends `ICommand`, so a command with a result is still a command — a
pre-interceptor written against `ICommand` sees both.

The result should be the *outcome of doing it*: the id that was created, the receipt. When a
command's result starts looking like a projection, that is usually two operations wearing one
name — return the id and let the caller query.

## Records, sealed, immutable

```csharp
public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name, decimal Price) : ICommand<Guid>;
```

A record gives you `with`, which is what makes a pre-interceptor rewrite a one-liner:

```csharp
=> ValueTask.FromResult(command with { Name = command.Name.Trim() });
```

`sealed` is worth the keystrokes. An unsealed command invites a subtype, and a subtype changes
which handler serves it.

## Inheritance

A base type is how a family shares cross-cutting treatment:

```csharp
public abstract record OrderCommand : ICommand;

public sealed record PlaceOrder(Guid CustomerId) : OrderCommand;
public sealed record CancelOrder(Guid Id) : OrderCommand;
```

An interceptor for `OrderCommand` now covers both, without naming either:

```csharp
public sealed class ValidateOrders : ICommandPreInterceptor<OrderCommand> { … }
```

Make the base `abstract` unless instances of it are real. A concrete base with no handler, whose
subtypes have handlers, is `ERGO006` — an instance of exactly that type would throw.

## Avoid `struct` commands

A value type has no contract variance, so a struct command reaches only registrations naming it
exactly. Every interceptor written against `ICommand` silently skips it. The allocation saved is
one small object per dispatch, which is rarely worth the surprise.

## One result type

A command declaring several result contracts cannot be given a compiled plan, because the result
is then named at the call site rather than by the message:

```csharp
// works, but takes the general path
public sealed record Ambiguous : ICommand<Guid>, ICommand<string>;
```

If you are here, you have two commands.

## Excluding it from the cross-cutting pipeline

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline]
public sealed record HealthProbe : ICommand;
```

That drops every covariantly matched interceptor — the ones registered against `ICommand` or a
base type. Directly registered interceptors and the handler still run. Name groups to drop only
some:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline("audit", "logging")]
public sealed record HealthProbe : ICommand;
```

## Keeping it out of bulk registration

```csharp
[DiscoveryKey("reporting")]
public sealed record RebuildReports : ICommand;
```

It registers only when a selection asks for `reporting`. See
[Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-concepts/discovery-keys).

## Where commands live

With their handlers, in the layer that serves them. A command and the code that handles it
change together, and the generator needs to see both.

## Next

[Defining a command handler](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-components/command/command-handler).

guides.description: Writing the one handler that serves a command, and dispatching it.

guides.title: Defining an event
guides.description: An event is a fact that already happened — and it does not have to implement anything to be one.
guides.body:
An event announces something that has already happened. Every matching subscriber runs, none of
them answers the publisher, and — unlike commands and queries — the message itself needs no
marker.

## A plain type is enough

```csharp
public sealed record OrderShipped(Guid OrderId, DateTimeOffset At);
```

That is a complete event. Writing a subscriber for it is what makes it one:

```csharp
public sealed class NotifyCustomer : IEventHandler<OrderShipped> { … }
```

An `IEventHandler<T>` signature is not evidence pointing at a message the generator then goes
looking for — it *is* the classification. So the project that declares your domain events needs
no reference to Ergosfare at all, and this works across assembly boundaries: the subscriber can
live anywhere.

{% aside type="note" %}
Nothing in the publish path ever needed the marker. `IEventHandler<TEvent>`,
`PublishAsync<TEvent>` and the broadcast dispatch are all declared over `notnull`, because a
broadcast carries no result and asks nothing of a message contract.
{% /aside %}

## Or declare `IEvent` deliberately

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Events.Abstractions;

public sealed record OrderShipped(Guid OrderId, DateTimeOffset At) : IEvent;
```

Both work identically at run time. The choice is about where the reference lands:

**Plain type** when the event belongs to your domain. A domain event is a fact about your
business, and the assembly declaring it should not need a mediator reference to say so. This is
the better default for a domain or contracts project.

**`IEvent`** when the type exists to be dispatched — an integration event, something shaped for
a queue, a message with no meaning outside the pipeline. The marker documents that, and it makes
the type discoverable on its own rather than only through a subscriber.

The one practical difference: a plain type nobody subscribes to is simply a class. It is not
registered, not rooted, and not reported — because from the outside it is not an event.

## Naming

Past tense, always. `OrderShipped`, not `ShipOrder`. An event names something that has already
happened; if the name reads as an instruction, you have a command.

```csharp
public sealed record OrderPlaced(Guid Id) ;      // event
public sealed record PlaceOrder(Guid Id) : ICommand<Guid>;   // command
```

## Carry what subscribers need

A subscriber that has to go and look everything up is a subscriber coupled to your read model:

```csharp
// forces every subscriber to query
public sealed record OrderShipped(Guid OrderId);

// enough to act on
public sealed record OrderShipped(Guid OrderId, string CustomerEmail, DateTimeOffset At);
```

The balance is against coupling every subscriber to a large payload. Carry the facts that were
true at the moment the event happened, and let subscribers query for the rest.

## Records, sealed, immutable

Several subscribers see the same instance. An immutable record means one of them cannot change
what the next one sees.

## Inheritance

```csharp
public abstract record OrderEvent
{
    public required Guid OrderId { get; init; }
}

public sealed record OrderPlaced  : OrderEvent;
public sealed record OrderShipped : OrderEvent;
```

A subscriber for `OrderEvent` receives both — and unlike commands, that is not a contest. A
broadcast delivers to every match, so a covariant subscriber is an ordinary participant:

```csharp
public sealed class AuditOrderEvents : IEventHandler<OrderEvent> { … }
```

## A publish nobody serves is a build error

```csharp
await mediator.PublishAsync(new OrderShipped(id, email, at));   // no subscriber anywhere
```

```
error ERGO005: This dispatch of 'OrderShipped' can never reach a handler … so the publish is
guaranteed to throw NoHandlerFoundException at runtime.
```

A publish requires at least one main handler, including when groups are used. A known group
set that selects none fails compilation with `ERGO024`. Dynamic groups selecting no handler
throw `NoHandlerFoundException` before interceptors run.

## Excluding it from the cross-cutting pipeline

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline("audit")]
public sealed record HeartbeatObserved(DateTimeOffset At) : IEvent;
```

## Next

[Defining an event handler](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-components/event/event-handler).
