guides.title: Modules and extensions
guides.description: The registration surface — AddErgosfare, the module builders, and what each call actually registers.
guides.body:
Registration is one call at the composition root, with a module per message family you use:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

## `AddErgosfare`

Registers the dispatch machinery — the mediators, the pipeline executors, the dependencies
factory — along with this container's view of the compiled composition table.

Modules are configured first and the registry finalized afterwards, so everything registered
during configuration is in place before the container is built.

## The module builders

Each module builder offers three ways to select what it registers.

### `AddGenerated()`

The bulk path, written by the generator. It names every construct that takes part in default
discovery — everything without a `[DiscoveryKey]`.

### `AddGenerated(pattern)`

Selects by discovery key: an exact key, or a prefix glob ending in `*`.

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(module => module
    .AddGenerated()
    .AddGenerated("reporting.*"))
```

Selections are a union, so overlapping patterns are safe.

### `Register<T>()` and `Register(typeof(T))`

Names one construct:

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(module => module
    .AddGenerated()
    .Register<AuditEverything>())
```

The type has to be named outright. A `Type` computed at run time is `ERGO018` — an error,
because a construct whose type is only known at run time gets no compiled pipeline, no frozen
composition and no plan.

{% aside type="note" %}
`EventModuleBuilder.Register<TEvent>()` accepts any `notnull` type, because an event message
does not have to implement a marker. The module check on the `Type` overload applies to
participants: registering a subscriber in the wrong module is still reported, while a message
belongs to no module and has nothing to check against.
{% /aside %}

## What each module registers

| Call | Adds |
|---|---|
| `AddCommandModule` | `ICommandMediator`, and the command participants selected |
| `AddQueryModule` | `IQueryMediator`, and the query participants selected |
| `AddEventModule` | `IEventMediator`, and the event participants selected |

`IMessageMediator` — the unified surface — comes from `AddErgosfare` itself.

Register only what you use. An application with no events adds no event module.

## Registry-level options

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .UseDefaultResultAdapter(typeof(ResultAdapter<>))
    .ForceMemoizedHandlers()
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

**`UseDefaultResultAdapter`** makes failures travel as values for every result slot the adapter
serves. An open generic is closed per slot it fits, at compile time — so the argument must be a
literal `typeof` (`ERGO019`) and a compilation names one adapter (`ERGO020`). Experimental —
`ERGOEXP001`.

**`ForceMemoizedHandlers`** keeps resolved participants instead of resolving one per dispatch.
For applications whose handlers are stateless and whose dependencies are singletons; wrong
anywhere a handler depends on something scoped.

**`Register(IModule)`** adds a module of your own, or one a package ships:

```csharp
.Register(new ReportingModule())
```

See [Modules](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-concepts/modules).

## Injecting a mediator

```csharp
public sealed class OrdersController(ICommandMediator commands, IQueryMediator queries)
{
    public Task<IResult> Post(PlaceOrder command) => …
}
```

Use the specific mediator where the code knows what it dispatches. `IMessageMediator` is for
code that genuinely does not — a queue consumer, a replay tool — and it costs you the
compile-time reachability judgments, because the static type at the call proves nothing about
which message arrives.

## Where to put this

At the composition root, once. That is where the generator judges reachability, and splitting
registration across several places is the usual way people lose those diagnostics. See
[Composition root and testing](/ergosfare.docs/preview/best-practices/composition-root).

guides.title: Defining a query
guides.description: Declaring a query that returns one result, or one that streams a sequence.
guides.body:
A query asks a question and changes nothing. It has exactly one handler, and it always produces
a result — a single value, or a stream of them.

## A single result

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Queries.Abstractions;

public sealed record GetProduct(Guid Id) : IQuery<ProductDto>;
```

There is no result-less query. A query with nothing to return is a command.

## A stream

```csharp
public sealed record SearchProducts(string Term) : IStreamQuery<ProductDto>;
```

The handler returns `IAsyncEnumerable<ProductDto>` and the caller reads it with `await foreach`.
Use it when the sequence is large enough that materialising it is the problem — a report, an
export, a paged scan feeding a consumer that processes as it goes.

For a bounded result set, `IQuery<IReadOnlyList<ProductDto>>` is simpler and usually right.

## Return a shape you own

A result is a contract. Returning your entity ties every caller to your persistence model:

```csharp
// leaks the aggregate
public sealed record GetOrder(Guid Id) : IQuery<Order>;

// a shape you control
public sealed record GetOrder(Guid Id) : IQuery<OrderDto>;
```

## Records, sealed, immutable

```csharp
public sealed record SearchProducts(string Term, int Page = 1) : IQuery<PagedResult<ProductDto>>;
```

Same reasoning as commands: `with` for interceptor rewrites, `sealed` so a subtype cannot
quietly change which handler serves it.

## Inheritance

```csharp
public abstract record TenantQuery<TResult> : IQuery<TResult>
{
    public required Guid TenantId { get; init; }
}

public sealed record GetProduct : TenantQuery<ProductDto>
{
    public required Guid Id { get; init; }
}
```

An interceptor written against the base covers the family — a tenant filter, for instance.

## Nullable results

A query that may find nothing should say so in the result type:

```csharp
public sealed record FindProduct(Guid Id) : IQuery<ProductDto?>;
```

That is better than throwing for the ordinary "not found" case, and it keeps the exception stage
for genuine failures. Note that a nullable reference result is what the `TResult?` in the
interceptor contracts refers to — see
[Exception interceptors](/ergosfare.docs/preview/cross-cutting-concerns/exception-interceptors).

## One result type

A query declaring several result contracts cannot be given a compiled plan, because the result
is named at the call site rather than by the message. It still works; it takes the general path.

## Excluding it from the cross-cutting pipeline

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline("audit")]
public sealed record GetHealth : IQuery<HealthDto>;
```

Useful for high-frequency queries where auditing every call would be noise.

## Streams do not get compiled plans

The streaming lane has no plan family, so a stream query always takes the general path. It is
correct and it works; it just does not get the straight-line body a single-result query gets.
The streaming surface is also the one part still under revision, which is why it has no typed
dispatch overloads yet.

## Next

[Defining a query handler](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-components/query/query-handler).

guides.description: Writing the handler that answers a query, streaming a sequence, and dispatching both.

guides.title: Compile-time discovery
guides.description: What the source generator finds, what it writes into your build, and what it deliberately refuses to guess at.
guides.body:
Ergosfare has no assembly scan. What another mediator discovers when your application starts,
this one works out while you compile, and writes into your assembly as code you can read.

## What gets found

The generator looks for types that reach a module marker — `ICommand`, `IQuery` or `IEvent`.
A message declares one itself. A handler or interceptor inherits one through the contract it
implements, so a single check finds all three.

It looks in two places:

**Your own compilation**, by visiting every type declaration with a base list.

**Referenced assemblies**, so a library's handlers register through the application that
consumes it. Only assemblies that themselves reference Ergosfare are read — nothing else can
carry a marker — and Ergosfare's own assemblies are skipped, since its contract interfaces
inherit the markers and would otherwise all match.

```xml
<!-- Turn the reference scan off for a project that does not want it -->
<ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences>false</ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences>
```

A type the generated code cannot name is reported rather than dropped in silence: `ERGO001`
for a `private`, `protected` or file-local type in your own code, `ERGO002` for an internal
type in a referenced assembly that has not granted you `InternalsVisibleTo`.

## What gets written

Three things land in `ErgosfareRegistrations.g.cs`.

### The registration

`AddGenerated()` names each construct through `typeof`, which is also what keeps the
trimming and AOT analyzers satisfied. Nothing here is convention-based, and nothing depends on
a type's name.

### The frozen composition table

One entry per message: its handler rows and its four interceptor stages, already in the order
they will run. This is the answer to "what serves this message", computed once at compile time
rather than assembled from descriptors on each dispatch.

The table describes the whole compiled world. Which of its rows a given container actually runs
is decided separately, by what that container registered — so two applications sharing a
library get the same table and different selections from it.

### The compiled plans

For pipelines whose shape is fully settled, the generator writes the body as a straight line of
calls: resolve, invoke, resolve, invoke. There is no loop over a descriptor list, and for
participants it can prove are plain transients, no container resolution either — the plan
constructs them with `new`.

A plan is always advisory. Before running one, the executor compares the composition it was
baked against with the pipeline the container actually composed, and falls back to the general
path on any difference. That is what makes the whole mechanism safe: a plan can lose you its
speedup, never change your behaviour.

## What it can prove about your code

Because the closure is visible at compile time, some questions that are normally runtime
surprises become build output. These run in the **composition root** — the project that sees
the whole application — which is why they appear when you build your executable rather than the
library that declared the handler.

| Diagnostic | Severity | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| `ERGO005` | error | This dispatch can never reach a handler. |
| `ERGO006` | warning | Only subtypes of the dispatched type are handled. |
| `ERGO007` | warning | No dispatch anywhere can reach this handler. |
| `ERGO010` | error | Two main handlers claim one message at the same level. |
| `ERGO018` | error | A `Register` call names its type at run time. |

`ERGO005` is the one people meet first:

```
error ERGO005: This dispatch of 'ArchiveOrder' can never reach a handler: neither
'ArchiveOrder' nor any of its subtypes in the compiled closure has a covering handler
registration, so the call is guaranteed to throw NoHandlerFoundException at runtime.
Register a handler for it or remove the dispatch.
```

It applies to publishing too. An event no subscriber in the compilation serves is a dead
dispatch like any other — writing the event and forgetting the subscriber is the ordinary way
to get there, and it used to compile in silence.

`ERGO007` points the other way, at a handler nothing can reach. Left alone it is a warning; opt
in and it becomes a size saving instead:

```xml
<ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>true</ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>
```

Unreachable handlers are then left out of the registration entirely — reported as `ERGO008` so
the exclusion is visible — and the linker can drop them.

## What it refuses to guess at

The judgments above are only sound while the picture is complete, and the generator is careful
about saying so. Each of these makes it stand down rather than report something it cannot
prove:

**A registration it cannot read.** `Register(someType)` where `someType` is computed at run
time. This is `ERGO018` at the registration itself, and the dead-dispatch judgment stays quiet
— the defect is the registration, not the dispatches downstream of it.

**Reference scanning turned off.** The composition is then knowingly incomplete, so no
closure-wide verdict holds.

**A missing manifest.** Each assembly records what it dispatches. If some Ergosfare-referencing
assembly in the closure carries none, dispatch sites may be invisible, and the
unreachable-handler side stays silent.

**An opaque dispatch site.** `SendAsync` through a variable typed as `ICommand` proves nothing
about which command arrives. Reachability can still reason about it in aggregate, but not
precisely. `ERGO009` reports these, off by default; teams who want every dispatch provable turn
it on:

```ini
dotnet_diagnostic.ERGO009.severity = warning
```

**A keyed or grouped registration.** Whether two such handlers are ever live together is a
container's choice, not a property of the types, so a contest between them is not reported.

## What stays at run time

Instance resolution. A handler is resolved from the dispatching scope for each dispatch, so
scoped dependencies behave as they do everywhere else. The generator decides *which* handler;
your container decides *which instance*.

## Seeing the output

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>true</EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>
  <CompilerGeneratedFilesOutputPath>$(BaseIntermediateOutputPath)generated</CompilerGeneratedFilesOutputPath>
</PropertyGroup>
```

The file is plain, readable C#. Reading it is the fastest way to answer "is my handler actually
registered", and the generated plan bodies show exactly what a dispatch will do.

## Next

- [Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-concepts/discovery-keys) — registering subsets
  of what was found.
- [Polymorphism](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-concepts/polymorphism) — how base contracts and
  covariant handlers resolve.
- [Working with diagnostics](/ergosfare.docs/preview/best-practices/diagnostics) — reading the
  ERGO codes as signals rather than noise.

guides.title: Discovery keys
guides.description: Keeping a construct out of bulk registration, and selecting it deliberately by key or pattern.
guides.body:
By default `AddGenerated()` registers everything the generator found. A discovery key
takes a construct out of that default and puts it behind a name you ask for explicitly.

## Declaring a key

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions.Attributes;

[DiscoveryKey("reporting")]
public sealed class RebuildReportsHandler : ICommandHandler<RebuildReports>
{
    public ValueTask HandleAsync(RebuildReports command, ErgosfareContext context) { … }
}
```

That handler is now invisible to a plain `AddGenerated()`. It registers only when
something asks for `reporting`:

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(module => module
    .AddGenerated()             // everything with no key
    .AddGenerated("reporting")) // and this one too
```

A type can carry several keys, and it registers when a selection matches any of them:

```csharp
[DiscoveryKey("reporting", "nightly")]
public sealed class RebuildReportsHandler : ICommandHandler<RebuildReports> { … }
```

## Assembly-level keys

Put the attribute on an assembly and every construct in it inherits the key:

```csharp
[assembly: DiscoveryKey("reporting")]
```

A type's own keys **replace** its assembly's rather than adding to them, so one type can opt
out of the assembly-wide grouping by naming its own.

## Selecting by pattern

A selection is an exact key, or a prefix glob ending in `*`:

```csharp
.AddGenerated("reporting.nightly")   // exactly this key
.AddGenerated("reporting.*")         // every key starting with "reporting."
.AddGenerated("*")                   // every keyed construct
```

Selections are a union, so chaining overlapping patterns is safe — a construct matched twice is
registered once.

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(module => module
    .AddGenerated()
    .AddGenerated("reporting.*")
    .AddGenerated("import.*"))
```

## What this is for

**A host that runs one job.** Several entry points share an assembly, and each registers the
slice it needs:

```csharp
// the API
.AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())

// the nightly worker
.AddCommandModule(module => module
    .AddGenerated()
    .AddGenerated("nightly.*"))
```

**A library shipping optional handlers.** Give them a key, and a consumer opts in by naming it
rather than by getting them whether they wanted them or not.

**An expensive interceptor you enable per environment.** A key keeps it out of the default
pipeline while leaving it one line away.

## Keys and groups are different questions

They are easy to confuse, and they answer opposite questions.

A **discovery key** decides whether a construct is *registered at all*. It is read at start-up,
by the composition root, and once the container is built the answer never changes.

A **group** decides whether a registered interceptor *runs on this dispatch*. It is named at
the call site, and can differ from one dispatch to the next.

```csharp
// registration time: is this thing in the container?
.AddGenerated("reporting.*")

// dispatch time: which of the registered interceptors run now?
await mediator.SendAsync(command, GroupSet.Of("audit"));
```

Use a key when the answer belongs to the deployment. Use a group when it belongs to the call.
See [Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/preview/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

## What a key costs you

A keyed construct is deliberately conditional, and the compile-time judgments respect that:

- It is left out of `ERGO010`, the contested-handler check. Whether two keyed handlers are ever
  registered together is a container's choice that nothing here can prove.
- It is exempt from `ERGO007`, the unreachable-handler warning, and from the handler trim.
- It does not take part in a compiled plan. Plans are built for the default pipeline, and a
  keyed participant may or may not be in the container that runs it.

None of this changes behaviour — a keyed handler dispatches exactly like any other. It means
the compiler has less to say about it, which is the trade you are making when you reach for a
key.

{% aside type="tip" %}
Because of that, keys are worth using sparingly. If a handler is always registered, leave it in
the default set where the diagnostics can see it.
{% /aside %}

## Hiding a type completely

`[DiscoveryKey]` keeps a type out of the *default* selection. `[ExcludeFromDiscovery]` keeps it
out of every selection, so the only way it reaches a container is a hand-written `Register`:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromDiscovery]
public sealed class ProbeHandler : ICommandHandler<Probe> { … }
```

An excluded type produces no registration and no diagnostics — the exclusion is what the author
asked for. It is still rooted for dispatch, because hiding a type from bulk collection says
nothing about whether it is dispatched, and a dispatch that has to close its generics
reflectively is a shape that works in development and fails under NativeAOT.

Put the attribute on an assembly and nothing in it is scanned at all:

```csharp
[assembly: ExcludeFromDiscovery]
```

guides.title: Modules
guides.description: What a module is, why commands, queries and events are separate ones, and how to write your own.
guides.body:
A module is a unit of registration. It owns a message family — its mediator, its participants,
and its half of the composition table — and you add the ones your application uses:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

An application with no events adds no event module, and pays for nothing it did not add.

## Why three

The three modules differ in **delivery**, not in machinery:

| Module | Handlers per message | Answers the caller |
|---|---|---|
| Commands | exactly one | with a result, or nothing |
| Queries | exactly one | with a result, or a stream of them |
| Events | every match | never |

Everything else — the four interceptor stages, the ordering rules, discovery, the compiled
plans — is shared. Splitting them keeps the delivery difference in the type system instead of
in a runtime flag: a `SendAsync` cannot accidentally fan out, and a `PublishAsync` cannot
accidentally return an answer.

It also keeps the boundary useful in your own code. `ICommandMediator` in a constructor says
this class issues instructions; `IQueryMediator` says it only asks questions. That is a
readable statement about the class, and it is enforced.

## What a module registers

Adding a module registers three things:

**Its mediator** — `ICommandMediator`, `IQueryMediator`, `IEventMediator` — so you can inject
it.

**Its participants**, from whatever the builder selected. `AddGenerated()` names them in
bulk; `Register<T>()` names one; a discovery-key pattern names a subset.

**Its view of the composition table.** The table itself is compiled into the assembly and
process-wide; what a module registers is which of its rows *this container* has selected.

That separation is why two applications sharing a handler library get the same compiled table
and different behaviour from it.

## The unified mediator

`IMessageMediator` dispatches any message, without knowing which module it belongs to:

```csharp
public sealed class QueueConsumer(IMessageMediator mediator)
{
    public ValueTask ProcessAsync(IMessage message, CancellationToken ct)
        => mediator.DispatchAsync(message, ct);
}
```

It is for code that genuinely does not know — a queue consumer, a replay tool — and it costs
you the compile-time judgments in return, because the static type at the call site proves
nothing about which message arrives. Prefer the specific mediator wherever the code does know.

When the result type is known at the call site, name it and the dispatch avoids constructing
its executor reflectively:

```csharp
var result = await mediator.DispatchAsync<PlaceOrder, Guid>(command, ct);
```

## Registering a module by hand

`AddCommandModule` and its siblings are extension methods over a small contract:

```csharp
public interface IModule
{
    void Build(IModuleConfiguration configuration);
}
```

`IModuleConfiguration` gives you the `IServiceCollection` and the container's composition
catalog. Implementing it directly is how a package ships its own registration:

```csharp
public sealed class ReportingModule : IModule
{
    public void Build(IModuleConfiguration configuration)
    {
        configuration.Services.AddSingleton<IReportRenderer, PdfRenderer>();
    }
}
```

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .Register(new ReportingModule())
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

{% aside type="note" %}
`Register(IModule)` takes a module, not a construct. It is a different method from the
`Register<T>()` on a module builder, which names a handler or interceptor. The calls a module
makes inside `Build` are the real registrations.
{% /aside %}

A plugin package generates this for you, along with the `Add<Name>` extension its consumers
call. See [Plugins](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/plugins).

## Registering across assemblies

A handler in a referenced library is found by the reference scan and registered through the
consuming application's `AddGenerated()`. Nothing extra is needed, and the library ships
no registration code of its own.

Two things are worth knowing:

**The library needs the generator too.** It records what it dispatches so the composition root
can reason about the whole closure.

**Internal handlers need a grant.** A library's `internal` handler is invisible to the
consumer's generated code unless the library grants `InternalsVisibleTo`, and that is reported
as `ERGO002` rather than silently skipped.

## Where to register

At the composition root, once. The compile-time judgments run there — it is the only place that
sees the whole application — and splitting registration across several places makes the picture
harder for both the compiler and the reader.

See [Composition root and testing](/ergosfare.docs/preview/best-practices/composition-root).

guides.title: Nested dispatch
guides.description: Dispatching from inside a handler — when to share the context, what the interceptors do, and how to keep it from becoming a hidden call graph.
guides.body:
A handler can dispatch. Injecting a mediator into a handler works exactly as it does anywhere
else, and the inner dispatch runs its own full pipeline:

```csharp
public sealed class PlaceOrderHandler(IEventMediator events, IOrderRepository repository)
    : ICommandHandler<PlaceOrder, Guid>
{
    public async ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(PlaceOrder command, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        var id = await repository.SaveAsync(command, context.CancellationToken);
        await events.PublishAsync(new OrderPlaced(id), context);
        return id;
    }
}
```

## Share the context, or do not

This is the one decision nested dispatch actually asks of you.

**Passing your context** makes the inner dispatch part of the same logical operation. It shares
your `Items`, so a correlation id set by an outer interceptor is visible to the inner one, and
it shares your cancellation token, so cancelling the outer work cancels the inner too.

```csharp
await events.PublishAsync(new OrderPlaced(id), context);
```

**Omitting it** gives the inner dispatch a fresh context. Use that when the inner work is
genuinely separate — its own state, its own cancellation:

```csharp
await events.PublishAsync(new OrderPlaced(id), cancellationToken);
```

The default is to pass it. An inner dispatch that is part of handling the outer message
normally belongs to the same operation, and losing the cancellation token by accident is a bug
that only shows up under load.

## Interceptors run every time

There is no "inner dispatch" mode. The nested call is a dispatch like any other, and every
interceptor matching the inner message runs:

```
PlaceOrder     pre → handler ─┐
                              │
OrderPlaced                   └→ pre → subscriber(s) → post → final
               post ← ────────┘
               final
```

That is usually what you want — the audit interceptor should see the inner event too. It is
also how a cross-cutting interceptor written against `ICommand` ends up running twice for one
request, which is worth knowing before you put something expensive in one.

## Watch for cycles

Nothing prevents a handler from dispatching a message whose handler dispatches back. There is
no cycle detection, and the compile-time judgments do not look for one — a cycle is a legal
shape that a state machine or a retry policy might genuinely want. Keeping the graph shallow is
on you.

{% aside type="tip" %}
If you find yourself two or three dispatches deep, that is usually a sign the work wants to be a
method call rather than a message. A message is for decoupling something that genuinely belongs
to another part of the application; using one to call code you own, in the same layer, buys the
indirection without the decoupling.
{% /aside %}

## Transactions do not nest for you

An inner dispatch runs in the same DI scope as the outer one, so a scoped `DbContext` is shared
and a transaction opened outside is still open inside. What does *not* happen is anything
automatic: nothing commits when the inner dispatch succeeds, and nothing rolls back when it
throws.

If you want a unit of work spanning a dispatch, own it explicitly — see the
[Unit of work recipe](/ergosfare.docs/preview/recipes/unit-of-work).

## Publishing events after the work, not during

A common shape is a handler that does its work and then announces it. Publishing *inside* the
transaction means a subscriber can observe a state that later rolls back:

```csharp
// the subscriber may act on an order that never existed
await repository.SaveAsync(order);
await events.PublishAsync(new OrderPlaced(order.Id), context);
await unitOfWork.CommitAsync();
```

Collect the events and publish after the commit instead, or hand them to an outbox. The
mediator has no opinion here — it dispatches when you tell it to — so the ordering is a design
decision you make rather than one the framework makes for you.

## What it costs

An inner dispatch is a dispatch: it looks up its plan, resolves its participants from the
current scope, and runs. It does not re-enter discovery or rebuild anything, and the context it
shares is the one already allocated. The cost is the pipeline you asked for and nothing on top
of it.

guides.title: Polymorphism
guides.description: How a handler or interceptor registered against a base type reaches a derived message, and which one wins when several could.
guides.body:
A participant registered against `ICommand` reaches every command. One registered against
`OrderCommand` reaches every order command. This is what makes cross-cutting work possible
without naming each message, and it follows one rule with one tiebreaker.

## Direct and covariant

A registration is **direct** when it names the exact type being dispatched, and **covariant**
when it names something the message is assignable to — a base class, or an interface it
implements.

```csharp
public abstract record OrderCommand : ICommand;
public sealed record PlaceOrder(Guid Id) : OrderCommand;

// direct for PlaceOrder
public sealed class PlaceOrderHandler : ICommandHandler<PlaceOrder> { … }

// covariant for PlaceOrder
public sealed class LogOrders : ICommandPreInterceptor<OrderCommand> { … }

// covariant for every command
public sealed class LogEverything : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
```

Dispatching a `PlaceOrder` runs all three: the two interceptors, then the handler.

## The rule for handlers: direct wins outright

A command or query has exactly one handler. When both a direct and a covariant candidate exist,
the direct one takes it — with no ambiguity and no warning, because that is what the priority
ladder says:

```csharp
public sealed class OrderCommandHandler : ICommandHandler<OrderCommand> { … }  // fallback
public sealed class PlaceOrderHandler   : ICommandHandler<PlaceOrder>   { … }  // wins
```

Dispatching `PlaceOrder` runs `PlaceOrderHandler`. `OrderCommandHandler` still serves every
*other* order command. This is the idiom for a default handler with specific overrides, and it
is fully supported by the compiled plans — a message with one direct handler gets a plan
regardless of what its base types carry.

**A tie is an error.** Two direct handlers, or two covariant ones with no direct handler to
settle it, means the ladder has nothing to choose between:

```
error ERGO010: Message 'PlaceOrder' is claimed by 2 main handlers at the same direct level
(App.PlaceOrderHandler, App.PlaceOrderHandlerV2) — the priority ladder has no tiebreaker
within a level, so every dispatch of this message throws MultipleHandlerFoundException at
runtime. Keep exactly one claimant on that level; a direct handler always beats covariant ones.
```

Reported at build time because it is provable at build time. Resolve it by deleting one, making
one direct, or putting them in different groups.

## The rule for interceptors: everyone runs

Interceptors are not exclusive. Every one that matches runs, ordered within its stage by
`[Weight]` descending, with direct registrations before covariant ones:

```csharp
[Weight(100)] public sealed class Authorize : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
[Weight(50)]  public sealed class Validate  : ICommandPreInterceptor<OrderCommand> { … }
```

## The rule for events: everyone runs, and that is the point

A publish delivers to every matching subscriber, so a covariant subscriber is an ordinary
participant rather than a competing claim:

```csharp
public sealed record OrderShipped(Guid Id) : OrderEvent;

public sealed class NotifyCustomer : IEventHandler<OrderShipped> { … }
public sealed class AuditOrders    : IEventHandler<OrderEvent>   { … }
```

Publishing an `OrderShipped` runs both.

## Value types have no variance

Contract variance is a reference-type feature. A `struct` message reaches only registrations
that name it exactly:

```csharp
public readonly record struct Ping : ICommand;

public sealed class LogEverything : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }  // does NOT see Ping
public sealed class PingHandler   : ICommandHandler<Ping>    { … }  // does
```

This is not an Ergosfare rule, it is how the runtime works — and the compile-time judgments
apply it the same way, so a struct message with no direct handler is `ERGO005` even when a
handler for `ICommand` exists.

{% aside type="caution" %}
Struct messages are worth avoiding for exactly this reason: every cross-cutting interceptor you
write silently skips them.
{% /aside %}

## Dispatching through a base type

The static type at the call site is what the compiler can see:

```csharp
OrderCommand command = GetNext();
await mediator.SendAsync(command);   // the runtime type's pipeline runs
```

The pipeline that runs belongs to the *runtime* type, which is what you want. But the compiler
now only knows it is an `OrderCommand`, so its reachability answers get correspondingly weaker.
Dispatching through `ICommand` or `object` weakens them further, and `ERGO009` reports those
sites when you turn it on.

That is a reason to keep the static type as specific as the code naturally allows — not a
reason to contort a call site that legitimately reads a message off a queue.

## Excluding covariant interceptors from a message

Sometimes a message should not get the cross-cutting treatment — a health probe that must not
be audited, a message whose logging would be noise:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline]
public sealed record HealthProbe : ICommand;
```

That drops every covariantly matched interceptor. Directly registered ones still run, and so
does the handler. Name groups to drop only some of them:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline("audit", "logging")]
public sealed record HealthProbe : ICommand;
```

The exclusion is resolved when the composition table is built, so it costs nothing per dispatch.
A message carrying it does not get a compiled plan.

## Generic messages

A generic message is keyed by its definition, so one table entry serves every instantiation:

```csharp
public sealed record Wrap<T>(T Value) : ICommand;

public sealed class WrapHandler<T> : ICommandHandler<Wrap<T>> { … }
```

The dispatch closes the participant over the arguments the message carries. What does *not*
work is a participant whose contract names a bare type parameter as its message:

```csharp
// ERGO016: closes over nothing, never runs
public sealed class ValidateAnything<TCommand> : ICommandPreInterceptor<TCommand>
    where TCommand : ICommand { … }
```

Participants are matched to messages by concrete type, and a concrete message carries no
arguments to close this one over. If the constraint admits compiled messages, the generator
closes the participant over each of them for you; if it admits none, `ERGO016` says so.

guides.title: Exception interceptors
guides.description: The stage that runs when something threw — answering the dispatch with a result, or letting the failure surface.
guides.body:
An exception interceptor runs when the handler or another interceptor threw. It can answer the
dispatch with a result instead of letting the exception escape.

## The contracts

```csharp
ICommandExceptionInterceptor                                  // every command
ICommandExceptionInterceptor<TCommand>                        // one command
ICommandExceptionInterceptor<TCommand, TResult>               // typed result
ICommandExceptionInterceptorFor<TException>                   // one exception type
ICommandExceptionInterceptorFor<TCommand, TException>
ICommandExceptionInterceptorFor<TCommand, TResult, TException>
```

Queries have the same set. Events have the ones without a result.

## Answering the dispatch

```csharp
public sealed class NotFoundToEmpty
    : IQueryExceptionInterceptor<GetProduct, ProductDto>
{
    public ValueTask<ProductDto> HandleAsync(
        GetProduct query, ProductDto? result, Exception exception, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        if (exception is NotFoundException)
            return ValueTask.FromResult(ProductDto.Empty);

        throw exception;
    }
}
```

Once an exception interceptor has run, the exception is considered handled and the pipeline
continues to the final stage. If none ran, it surfaces to the caller.

## Nullable in, non-nullable out

Look at the signature again: `ProductDto? result` comes in, `ValueTask<ProductDto>` goes out.
The asymmetry is deliberate.

**The parameter is nullable** because the handler may have thrown before producing anything.
There genuinely may be no result yet.

**The return is not** because the caller locked the result type at the call site. A dispatch of
`IQuery<ProductDto>` promised a `ProductDto`, and no stage downstream may hand back a `null`
the caller never asked for — that would arrive in a non-nullable slot with the exception gone,
which is the worst of both.

So an interceptor that cannot produce a result should not claim the failure:

```csharp
// right: let it surface
throw exception;

// wrong: it does not compile, and it should not
return ValueTask.FromResult<ProductDto>(null);
```

Code that wants to model absence models it in the value — an `Option`, a `Result<T>`, an empty
instance — rather than in the nullability of the result slot.

{% aside type="note" %}
The erased core contracts still return a nullable result, because they serve the void lane too,
where an empty slot legitimately reaches this stage as `null`. It is the typed result contracts
that were tightened.
{% /aside %}

## Filtering by exception type

The `For` variants narrow to one exception type. That reads better than an `is` check, and it
lets the compiled plan bake the test:

```csharp
public sealed class HandleTimeouts
    : ICommandExceptionInterceptorFor<PlaceOrder, Guid, TimeoutException>
{
    public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(
        PlaceOrder command, Guid? result, TimeoutException exception, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        _metrics.Increment("order.timeout");
        return ValueTask.FromResult(Guid.Empty);
    }
}
```

An interceptor whose filter does not match is not run at all, and does not count as having
handled anything. If every interceptor in the stage is filtered and none matches, the exception
surfaces exactly as if the stage were empty.

## Aborts are not failures

`ExecutionAbortedException` does not reach this stage. An abort is a deliberate stop, so the
exception stage and the final stage are both skipped and the signal travels to the caller. You
never need to filter it out.

## Ordering

`[Weight]` descending, direct before covariant. With several interceptors that could all match,
put the specific ones first:

```csharp
[Weight(100)] public sealed class HandleTimeouts   : ICommandExceptionInterceptorFor<PlaceOrder, Guid, TimeoutException> { … }
[Weight(10)]  public sealed class HandleEverything : ICommandExceptionInterceptor<PlaceOrder, Guid> { … }
```

## Typical uses

**Translating an infrastructure failure into a domain answer** — a timeout into an empty page,
a not-found into a null object.

**Enriching before rethrowing**, adding context and letting the original surface:

```csharp
_logger.LogError(exception, "Dispatching {Command} failed", command.GetType().Name);
throw exception;
```

**Converting to a result carrier**, when your application carries failures as values. Note that
if you configure a default result adapter, the framework already does this for the slots the
adapter serves — see
[Configuring Ergosfare](/ergosfare.docs/preview/getting-started/configuring).

## What does not belong here

**Cleanup.** Use a final interceptor, which runs on both paths.

**Swallowing everything.** A broad interceptor that catches every exception and returns a
default turns every bug into a silent wrong answer. Filter to the exceptions you actually know
how to answer.

**Retries.** This stage runs once, after the pipeline. A retry wants to re-run the work, which
belongs in a decorator on the dependency that fails, or in the caller.

guides.title: Final interceptors
guides.description: The stage that always runs — on success, on failure, and the one case where it does not.

guides.title: Groups and weights
guides.description: Ordering interceptors within a stage, and selecting which of them run on a given dispatch.
guides.body:
Two attributes shape a pipeline. `[Weight]` decides **order** within a stage; `[Group]` decides
**membership** — which interceptors run on this particular dispatch.

## Weights

Within a stage, participants run by weight descending. Equal weights fall back to direct
registrations before covariant ones, then to type name:

```csharp
[Weight(100)] public sealed class Authorize : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
[Weight(50)]  public sealed class Validate  : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
[Weight(10)]  public sealed class Log       : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
```

Undeclared means `0`. Weight is a `uint`, so it does not go negative — leave room by starting
your important ones high rather than trying to go below the default.

Ordering is settled when the composition is compiled, so it costs nothing per dispatch and
cannot be rearranged at a call site.

{% aside type="tip" %}
Declare weights whenever two interceptors genuinely depend on running in an order. Leaving both
at the default and relying on the type-name tiebreaker means renaming a class can reorder your
pipeline.
{% /aside %}

## Groups

A group puts an interceptor in a named set. A dispatch names the sets it wants, and only those
interceptors run:

```csharp
[Group("audit")]
public sealed class WriteAuditRow : ICommandFinalInterceptor { … }
```

```csharp
await mediator.SendAsync(command, GroupSet.Of("audit"));
```

An interceptor with no `[Group]` belongs to the **default** group. A dispatch that names no
group asks for the default one — so the ordinary case, no attribute and no argument, is just
the default group talking to itself.

A type can be in several groups, and it runs when any of them is requested:

```csharp
[Group("audit", "compliance")]
public sealed class WriteAuditRow : ICommandFinalInterceptor { … }
```

## Naming a set at the call

Every mediator uses `GroupSet` for group arguments. A string converts to a single-group set;
a collection expression creates a set with the listed names:

```csharp
await mediator.SendAsync(command, "audit");
await mediator.SendAsync(command, ["audit", "metrics"]);
await mediator.SendAsync(command, []);                         // default group
await mediator.SendAsync(command, "");                         // a group named ""

GroupSet reporting = ["audit", "metrics"];
await mediator.SendAsync(command, reporting);                  // reuse a set
```

`[]`, `GroupSet.Empty` and omitting groups select the default group. `""` and `[""]`
select the empty-string group, which requires a matching main handler. Known unmatched
selections fail compilation; dynamic unmatched selections throw `NoHandlerFoundException`.

There are no separate string, array, list or enumerable dispatch overloads. To use names
from a dynamic collection, materialize a `GroupSet` explicitly with `GroupSet.Of(array)` or
`GroupSet groups = [.. names]`. Reuse the set when dispatching repeatedly.

`GroupSet` implements `IReadOnlyList<string>`: its names can still be indexed or enumerated.

## Groups do not touch handlers

A group narrows the **interceptors**. The handler is chosen the same way regardless:

```csharp
// same handler either way; different interceptors around it
await mediator.SendAsync(command);
await mediator.SendAsync(command, GroupSet.Of("import"));
```

The one exception is when handlers themselves carry groups, which is how you express two
handlers as alternatives rather than a contest:

```csharp
[Group("v1")] public sealed class PlaceOrderV1 : ICommandHandler<PlaceOrder, Guid> { … }
[Group("v2")] public sealed class PlaceOrderV2 : ICommandHandler<PlaceOrder, Guid> { … }
```

Neither is selected by the default set, so an ungrouped dispatch of `PlaceOrder` finds no
handler — and that is `ERGO005` at build time. Naming a group is then not optional, which is
usually what you want when you did this deliberately.

## What it costs

Group sets are part of what keys a compiled plan, so a message dispatched under two different
sets gets a plan for each — each one a straight line with exactly the participants that set
selects. Filtering does not happen per dispatch.

When a dispatch names a set the compiler cannot read — a variable or a computed group set — the
message gets one plan that carries every participant and evaluates each one's membership at
run time. That is still a compiled plan; it just does the selection you deferred.

```csharp
// readable: each set gets its own straight-line plan
await mediator.SendAsync(command, GroupSet.Of("audit"));

// not readable: one plan, membership decided per call
await mediator.SendAsync(command, _configuredGroups);
```

Both are correct. The first is faster, and it is worth preferring where the set really is a
constant.

{% aside type="note" %}
A `static readonly GroupSet` is readable too — the generator follows one hop through a named
reference, which is exactly the recommended way to name a set once and reuse it.
{% /aside %}

## Typical uses

**An expensive pipeline you opt into.** Put full auditing in a group, and name it on the
operations that need it.

**Environment-specific behaviour**, without a flag inside every interceptor.

**Import and replay paths.** A bulk import wants validation but not notification; a replay
wants neither. Groups let one handler serve all three.

```csharp
[Group("import")] public sealed class SkipNotifications : ICommandPreInterceptor { … }
```

## Groups or discovery keys

They answer different questions, and mixing them up is the usual source of confusion.

A **discovery key** decides whether something is *registered at all*. Read once, at start-up, by
the composition root.

A **group** decides whether a registered interceptor *runs on this dispatch*. Read at the call
site, and it can differ per call.

Use a key when the answer belongs to the deployment; a group when it belongs to the call. See
[Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-concepts/discovery-keys).

## Excluding covariant interceptors from a message

For a message that should not get the cross-cutting treatment at all, the exclusion goes on the
message rather than on every interceptor:

```csharp
[ExcludeFromPipeline]                      // drops every covariantly matched interceptor
public sealed record HealthProbe : ICommand;

[ExcludeFromPipeline("audit", "logging")]  // drops only those groups
public sealed record HealthProbe : ICommand;
```

Directly registered interceptors and the handler still run. The exclusion is resolved when the
composition table is built, so it costs nothing per dispatch — but a message carrying it gets
no compiled plan.

guides.title: Post-interceptors
guides.description: The stage that runs after a successful handler — observing and reshaping the result.

guides.title: Pre-interceptors
guides.description: The stage that runs before the handler — rejecting, enriching, and rewriting the message.

guides.title: Configuring Ergosfare
guides.description: What you can tell the registry — modules, result adapters, memoized handlers — and what is decided by the build instead.
guides.body:
Configuration is deliberately small. Most of what a mediator usually exposes as a setting is
decided at compile time here, so the registry is left with the questions that genuinely belong
to an application rather than to a type.

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

`AddErgosfare` wires the module mediators, dispatch engine and selected participants into DI.
Assembly scanning finds candidates; only types selected by `AddGenerated` and explicit
`Register<T>()` declarations enter validation and generated plans. These declarations are a
compile-time union, not runtime branches selecting different pipeline definitions.

`ExcludeFromDiscovery` excludes automatic selection. Explicit `Register<T>()` still selects
the full participant, with the same group, constructor and adapter validation. A referenced library selects participants only when its configuration method is called;
its generated selection manifest carries those declarations to the composition root.
After initialization the catalog rejects registration and descriptor changes.

## Choosing what a module registers

Inside a module builder, three shapes are available.

**`AddGenerated()`** is the bulk path and what most applications call. It is a public builder method, owned by Ergosfare. The generator supplies
the selected types; no generated namespace is required for these calls.

**`AddGenerated(pattern)`** selects by discovery key instead — an exact key, or a prefix
glob ending in `*`:

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(module => module
    .AddGenerated()
    .AddGenerated("reporting.*"))
```

Selections are a union, so chaining overlapping patterns is safe. See
[Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-concepts/discovery-keys).

**`Register<T>()` / `Register(typeof(T))`** names one construct. Use it for something
deliberately kept out of bulk discovery.

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(module => module
    .AddGenerated()
    .Register<AuditEverything>())
```

{% aside type="caution" %}
A `Register` call has to name its type outright. Passing a `Type` computed at run time is
`ERGO018`, and it is an error rather than a warning: a construct whose type is only known at
run time gets no compiled pipeline, no frozen composition and no plan, so the registration
cannot mean what it appears to mean.
{% /aside %}

## A default result adapter

By default a failing pipeline throws. If your application carries failures as values instead —
`Result<T>`, or a carrier of your own — tell the registry once and every result slot that
adapter serves stops throwing:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .UseDefaultResultAdapter(typeof(ResultAdapter<>))
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

An open generic is closed per result slot it fits. Naming a closed type binds that one slot.

The closing happens at compile time, which puts two rules on the call. The argument must be a
literal `typeof` the compilation can resolve — a variable or a computed type is `ERGO019` —
and a compilation names one default adapter, a second one naming something else being
`ERGO020`. An adapter that serves several result families does so through several
`IResultAdapter<TResult>` implementations, not through a second call.

Configuring a default makes value-carried failure the application's contract, and the compiler
holds you to it: a result-bearing message whose result no adapter serves is `ERGO013`, because
its pipeline would keep throwing while the rest of the application stopped expecting that. If
that is deliberate, say so on the message with `[IgnoreResultAdapter]`, which turns the error
into a visible warning instead.

{% aside type="note" %}
The result-adapter surface is experimental and marked `ERGOEXP001`. See
[Experimental APIs](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/experimental-apis).
{% /aside %}

## Memoized handlers

By default a handler instance is resolved from the dispatching scope for every dispatch, which
is what makes scoped dependencies work. `ForceMemoizedHandlers()` keeps resolved participants
instead:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .ForceMemoizedHandlers()
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

This is for applications whose handlers are genuinely stateless and whose dependencies are
singletons — a background worker draining a queue, say. It is the wrong choice anywhere a
handler depends on something scoped, because the instance it captured outlives the scope that
produced it.

## Installing a plugin

A plugin package generates its own `Add<Name>` extension on the registry:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddTiming()
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

When the plugin declares options, that call takes them. Plugins are experimental —
`ERGOEXP002` — and covered in [Plugins](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/plugins).

## What is not configurable, and why

Some things that other mediators expose as settings are decided by the build here:

**Which handler serves a message.** A property of the types, resolved once by the generator.
Two handlers claiming one message at the same level is `ERGO010` at build time rather than an
exception on the first dispatch.

**Interceptor order.** `[Weight]` on the type, direct registrations before covariant ones.
Ordering is part of what gets compiled, so it cannot be rearranged per call.

**Whether a dispatch with no handler throws.** Every lane, including events, requires a
selected main handler. Provable failures are `ERGO005` or `ERGO024` at build time; dynamic
group selections without a handler throw `NoHandlerFoundException`. This is not configurable.

**Per-dispatch pipeline options.** A dispatch takes the message, a group set, a context and a
cancellation token. Anything that would change the pipeline's shape is part of what keys the
compiled plan, so it is named at the call as a group rather than passed as an option. See
[Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/preview/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

## Build-level settings

A few things are MSBuild properties rather than registry calls, because they affect what gets
compiled:

| Property | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ErgosfareCompositionRoot` | output kind | Marks the project whose closure is judged. |
| `ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences` | `true` | Whether referenced assemblies are scanned for handlers. |
| `ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers` | `false` | Leaves unreachable handlers out of the registration. |

See [Installation](/ergosfare.docs/preview/getting-started/installation) for where each one
belongs.

guides.title: Installation
guides.description: Which packages to install for the preview line, what each one carries, and the target frameworks they support.
guides.body:
The preview line ships as `-preview` pre-releases. Your package manager will not offer them
unless you ask for pre-releases explicitly.

## The one package most applications need

`Stella.Ergosfare` is a facade: it references the three modules, their dependency-injection
extensions, and the source generator. Installing it is enough to write a handler and dispatch
a message.

```bash
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare --prerelease
```

{% aside type="tip" %}
Pin the exact version in a preview line rather than floating. The surface can change between
pre-releases, and a floating reference turns that into a surprise at restore time.
{% /aside %}

## Or the pieces, if you split by layer

Most applications that split into layers want the message contracts in one project and the
registration in another. Reference only what each project actually needs:

| Package | What it carries | Where it belongs |
|---|---|---|
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions` | `ErgosfareContext`, the interceptor contracts, the attributes | anywhere a handler or interceptor is written |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions` | `ICommand`, `ICommandHandler<>`, `ICommandMediator` | the layer that declares commands |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Queries.Abstractions` | `IQuery<>`, `IStreamQuery<>`, `IQueryHandler<>`, `IQueryMediator` | the layer that declares queries |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Events.Abstractions` | `IEvent`, `IEventHandler<>`, `IEventMediator` | the layer that declares events |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.*.Extensions.MicrosoftDependencyInjection` | `AddCommandModule`, `AddQueryModule`, `AddEventModule` | the composition root only |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator` | the generator itself | every project that declares handlers, and the composition root |

The generator is an analyzer reference, so it carries no runtime dependency:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator" Version="…">
  <PrivateAssets>all</PrivateAssets>
  <IncludeAssets>runtime; build; native; contentfiles; analyzers; buildtransitive</IncludeAssets>
</PackageReference>
```

An event message needs no reference at all. A plain domain type becomes an event the moment a
subscriber names it, so the project declaring your domain events can stay free of Ergosfare
entirely — see
[Defining an event](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-components/event/event-definition).

## Target frameworks

The packages target **net9.0**, **net10.0** and **net11.0**. The generator itself targets
`netstandard2.0`, as Roslyn analyzers must, so it loads into any SDK new enough to build those.

C# 13 or later is required for the language features the generated code uses. That comes with
the SDKs above, so setting `<LangVersion>` by hand is not necessary.

## Where the generator has to run

The generator does two separate jobs, and it needs to be referenced in both places:

**In a project that declares handlers**, it finds them and records what that assembly
dispatches, so a library carries its own manifest for consumers to read.

**In the composition root**, it writes `AddGenerated()` and the compiled plans, and — only
here, where the whole application is visible — it judges reachability. That is why ERGO005 and
ERGO007 appear when you build the executable rather than the library that declared the handler.

Ergosfare treats an application project as a composition root by default. If your root is a
library — a test host, a plugin container — say so:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ErgosfareCompositionRoot>true</ErgosfareCompositionRoot>
</PropertyGroup>
```

## MSBuild properties

| Property | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ErgosfareCompositionRoot` | output kind | Marks this project as the composition root, or forces it off. |
| `ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences` | `true` | Whether referenced assemblies are scanned for handlers. |
| `ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers` | `false` | Leaves handlers no dispatch reaches out of the registration, so the linker can drop them. |

Reference scanning is what lets a library's handlers register through the application that
consumes it. Turning it off leaves the picture deliberately incomplete, so the whole-closure
diagnostics stand down with it.

## Verifying the install

Write one handler, build, and look at the generated file. In an IDE it appears under
*Dependencies → Analyzers → Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator* as
`ErgosfareRegistrations.g.cs`. Or dump it to disk:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>true</EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>
  <CompilerGeneratedFilesOutputPath>$(BaseIntermediateOutputPath)generated</CompilerGeneratedFilesOutputPath>
</PropertyGroup>
```

If your handler's type name appears there, discovery found it. If it does not, the most common
reasons are that the type is `private` or file-local — which is reported as ERGO001 — or that
it lives in a referenced assembly with scanning turned off.

## Next

[Quick start](/ergosfare.docs/preview/getting-started/quick-start) walks a command, a query, an
event and an interceptor end to end.

guides.title: Introduction
guides.description: Ergosfare is a source-generated mediator for commands, queries and events in .NET, where the shape of a dispatch is decided at compile time rather than discovered at run time.
guides.body:
Ergosfare is a mediator for CQRS-style messaging in .NET. Commands, queries and events all
travel one pipeline model, and the design premise is a single sentence: **the shape of a
dispatch is decided while you compile, not while you run.**

A Roslyn source generator reads your assembly and the ones it references, works out which
handlers and interceptors serve each message, and writes that answer into your build as a
table. What a dispatch then does at run time is walk a list that was already assembled — no
assembly scan, no reflection over handler types, no `MakeGenericType`, and no per-dispatch
allocation to carry the context.

{% aside type="caution" %}
You are reading the **preview line**, built from the
[`preview` branch](https://github.com/stellayazilim/Ergosfare/tree/preview). Packages ship as
`-preview` pre-releases and the surface can change between them. The stable line is
[v2 at the site root](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/introduction).
{% /aside %}

## What it looks like

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions;
using Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions;

public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name) : ICommand<Guid>;

public sealed class CreateProductHandler : ICommandHandler<CreateProduct, Guid>
{
    public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(Guid.NewGuid());
}
```

Register once, at your composition root:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

And dispatch:

```csharp
var id = await mediator.SendAsync(new CreateProduct("Bench"));
```

`AddGenerated()` is written by the generator. It names every construct it found, so
nothing here scans an assembly at start-up and nothing depends on a naming convention.

## What the compiler already knows

Most of what a mediator usually decides per dispatch is knowable earlier, and Ergosfare moves
it there:

**Which handler serves this message** is a property of the types, not of the call. The
generator resolves it once and bakes the answer.

**Which interceptors run, and in what order** is the same question. Each message gets a
*composition* — its handler rows and its four interceptor stages, already sorted — and for the
pipelines it can prove exactly, the generator writes the body as a straight line of calls.

**Whether a dispatch can work at all** is answerable too, and this is the part that changes how
the framework feels. A `SendAsync` for a command nothing in your compilation handles is not a
runtime surprise; it is a build error:

```
error ERGO005: This dispatch of 'ArchiveOrder' can never reach a handler: neither
'ArchiveOrder' nor any of its subtypes in the compiled closure has a covering handler
registration, so the call is guaranteed to throw NoHandlerFoundException at runtime.
```

The same judgment runs the other way: a handler no dispatch can reach is reported, and can be
trimmed from the registration entirely. See
[Compile-time discovery](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery).

## What you still decide at run time

The compiler decides the *shape*. Your container decides the *selection*: which of the rows in
that table your application actually registered, and which instances they resolve to. A
handler is resolved from the dispatching scope like any other service, so scoped dependencies
behave the way they do everywhere else in your application.

A dispatch can also narrow the pipeline per call with **groups**, which select a subset of the
interceptors — the audit pipeline, the import pipeline — without changing the handler. See
[Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/preview/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

## Three modules, one pipeline

| Module | Message | Handlers | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commands | `ICommand`, `ICommand<TResult>` | exactly one | none, or `TResult` |
| Queries | `IQuery<TResult>`, `IStreamQuery<TResult>` | exactly one | `TResult`, or a stream of them |
| Events | `IEvent`, or any type a subscriber names | every match | none |

They differ in delivery, not in machinery: all three build the same four interceptor stages
around the handler, and all three are compiled the same way.

An event message does not have to implement anything. Writing an `IEventHandler<OrderShipped>`
is what makes `OrderShipped` an event, so a domain type in a project with no Ergosfare
reference can be published as-is. See
[Defining an event](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-components/event/event-definition).

## Native AOT

The framework targets a published NativeAOT application as a first-class case rather than a
best effort. What makes that possible is the same compile-time work: generic instantiations
are closed in generated code, so the dispatch path has nothing left to construct reflectively.
See [Native AOT and trimming](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/aot-and-trimming).

## Where to go next

- [Installation](/ergosfare.docs/preview/getting-started/installation) — packages and the
  target frameworks they support.
- [Quick start](/ergosfare.docs/preview/getting-started/quick-start) — a command, a query, an
  event and an interceptor, end to end.
- [Core concepts](/ergosfare.docs/preview/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery) — what the
  generator does, and what it refuses to guess at.
- [Best practices](/ergosfare.docs/preview/best-practices/messages-and-handlers) — how to shape
  messages, and where cross-cutting work belongs.
